gloss: negation, non-being, absence — the foundational negative of Chinese philosophy, recruited by Chan as a pedagogical tool rather than an ontological claim
notes: Unlike Sanskrit śūnya, 無 is a native Chinese negative with no Sanskrit original. Chan teachers shaped its meaning through use, not translation.

gloss: emptiness — the absence of svabhāva (inherent, independent self-existence) in all phenomena
notes: Central term of Madhyamaka philosophy (Nāgārjuna). Things are empty not because they don't exist but because they exist only interdependently. The Chinese 空 carries this but flattens the relational logic.

gloss: citta: mind, consciousness, the thinking-feeling organ; hṛdaya: heart, the physical and spiritual center
notes: Chinese 心 conflates both Sanskrit terms into one, reflecting a Chinese conceptual unity that neither Sanskrit term alone captures.

gloss: mārga: path, road, the way to liberation; tao: the Way — the underlying ordering principle of reality in Daoist and Confucian thought
notes: Buddhist translators used the pre-existing Chinese 道 (tao) to render Sanskrit mārga, inheriting centuries of Daoist and Confucian resonance. Chan exploited this layering deliberately.

gloss: the love of wisdom; systematic rational inquiry into the nature of existence, knowledge, value, and mind
notes: Nishi Amane encountered the term primarily through Dutch philosophy during his studies in the Netherlands. His coinage frames Western philosophy through the lens of Confucian sage-wisdom.

gloss: an abstract collective of individuals bound by shared norms and institutions — distinct from the state, the family, and mere population
notes: A specifically modern Western sociological concept. Classical Chinese thought organized social reality through relational categories (the five relationships), not through an abstract collective sphere.

gloss: rule by the people; a system of government in which political authority derives from and is exercised by the citizenry
notes: The classical Chinese compound 民主 meant 'lord of the people' (paternalistic), not 'rule by the people.' Repurposing it for democracy inverts the classical political relationship.

gloss: awakening, enlightenment — the direct, unmediated seeing of reality as it is; the cognitive event that constitutes liberation
notes: From the Sanskrit root budh- (to awake, to know). Bodhi is not a belief or a doctrine but an event — the sudden or gradual opening of direct perception of the nature of mind and phenomena. Sambodhi (complete awakening) and anuttarā-samyak-sambodhi (unsurpassed, complete, perfect awakening) are standard formal terms. The Chinese 悟 renders the ordinary Buddhist usage of bodhi as the transformative recognition event, while 覚 (kaku) tends to carry more of the gradual-cultivation sense of Sanskrit bodhi as ongoing wakefulness.

gloss: intentional action — volitional deed that conditions the stream of consciousness and future experience
notes: From Sanskrit root kṛ- (to do, to make). In Buddhist usage, karma is not fate or cosmic justice but a psychological-causal claim: it is specifically cetanā (intention, volition) that constitutes karma, not the physical act alone. The three modes of karma — bodily (kāya-karman), verbal (vāk-karman), mental (mano-karman) — establish that thought itself is an action with karmic force. The Chinese 業 captures the deed/action sense precisely but loses the specific emphasis on intention as the defining factor; Buddhist commentators in both Chinese and Japanese traditions were careful to restore this qualification.

gloss: systematic empirical inquiry into the natural world; organized, methodical knowledge production
notes: The German Wissenschaft (systematic organized knowledge, including humanistic disciplines) fits the coinage 科学 better than English 'science,' which by the mid-19th century meant primarily natural science.

gloss: seeing one's nature — the direct perceptual breakthrough into Buddha-nature; the foundational Chan awakening event expressed as a transitive act of sight
notes: Not a translation from Sanskrit: 見性 is a Chan Chinese formulation crystallized in the Platform Sutra slogan 見性成仏 ('seeing one's nature, becoming Buddha'). The Sanskrit closest to it would be buddha-dhātu-darśana (seeing the Buddha-element) or ātma-darśana (seeing the self/nature), but Chan teachers developed the concept independently from the formulation 'what is one's nature?' as a meditation question. The critical doctrinal tension is whether 見 (seeing) implies a subject that sees and an object (性, nature) that is seen — Dōgen problematizes this in 'Busshō,' arguing that if Buddha-nature is all-encompassing, the subject-object grammar of 見性 must be dissolved.

gloss: informal assembly — a less formal dharma dialogue in which the teacher offers a short talk and holds exchange with attendees, contrasted with the grand formality of jōdō
notes: The complement of 上堂 in the Chan/Zen monastic schedule. Where jōdō is the fully formal convocation with the abbot ascending the high seat in the dharma hall, shōsan is a more relaxed, intimate gathering in which the teacher may speak briefly and then engage in extended question-and-answer. The format is typically held in a less formal space or without the full ceremonial apparatus of jōdō. In contemporary Western Zen practice, shōsan has been widely adopted as a public question-and-answer format, sometimes as an alternative to dokusan for practitioners who may not have a formal koan practice.

gloss: ascending the hall — the formal convocation in which the abbot mounts the high seat in the dharma hall and addresses the full assembly, sometimes engaging in spontaneous mondō
notes: A Chan/Zen monastic institution traceable to at least the Tang dynasty. The jōdō is one of the most formal ritual occasions in the Zen monastic calendar: the abbot ascends the high seat (高座, kōza) in the dharma hall (法堂, hattō), sometimes incenses, and delivers a formal address or engages in spontaneous question-and-answer with members of the assembly. The format is distinct from teishō (which is commentary on a specific koan or text) in that jōdō may be more spontaneous, more responsive to the occasion, and more interactive. The Song-dynasty recorded sayings collections (語録, goroku) preserve large numbers of jōdō addresses, making the form one of the primary literary genres of Chan/Zen.

gloss: going to Zen — private interview with a master emphasizing the student's initiative in approaching the teacher; functionally overlapping with dokusan but foregrounding the movement of approach rather than the privacy of the encounter
notes: Closely related to 独参 (dokusan) and sometimes used interchangeably. The distinction, when observed, is one of emphasis: dokusan foregrounds the private one-on-one character of the interview; sanzen foregrounds the student's initiative in going to the master. In institutional practice some lineages use sanzen as the primary term for the private interview during sesshin, while others reserve dokusan for the specific Rinzai format. The compound 参禅 can also function more broadly as 'going to [study] Zen' — the student's initial approach to a Zen master for training.

gloss: private one-on-one interview with a Zen master — the institutional form of the intimate encounter in which the student presents understanding and the master evaluates, the core mechanism of Rinzai koan training
notes: A Chan/Zen institutional form without a direct Sanskrit antecedent. Dokusan is the mechanism through which the koan curriculum is worked through: the student meditates on the koan, develops a response or a demonstration of understanding, and presents it to the master in a private interview. The master accepts, rejects, or redirects the student's presentation. The interview is confidential — what passes between master and student in dokusan is not shared with others — and the format is brief and concentrated, typically lasting only a few minutes. In Rinzai sesshin, dokusan is offered multiple times daily, and the rhythm of sitting-and-interview, sitting-and-interview creates the pressure that drives the koan practice forward.

gloss: formal dharma presentation — a master's commentary on a koan or Zen text, understood as a demonstration of realized insight rather than an explanation; the vocal form that Zen teaching takes in its most formal register
notes: A Chan/Zen institutional form with no direct Sanskrit antecedent. The compound 提唱 — to hold up and proclaim — names the master's public presentation of a koan or text as a demonstration of realized understanding. The teishō is not a lecture: it does not explain the koan's meaning in intellectual terms but enacts the insight the koan points at through the master's voice, timing, and presence. In the Rinzai tradition teishō is closely associated with the koan curriculum: the master presents a koan and its associated commentaries as a living demonstration. In the Sōtō tradition teishō has a broader range, sometimes covering doctrinal exposition as well as koan commentary. In both cases the distinction from ordinary lecturing is maintained: the audience is invited not to learn information but to receive the demonstration.

gloss: question-and-answer — the formal dialogic exchange between master and student; the mode underlying most koan records, in which the student's question is met by the master's response that refuses, shatters, or redirects the question's conceptual frame
notes: Not a translation from Sanskrit but a Chinese compound naming the dialogic form that Chan/Zen developed as its primary pedagogical vehicle. The koan literature — Gateless Gate, Blue Cliff Record, Book of Serenity — is almost entirely composed of recorded 問答 exchanges. The form is distinctive: unlike Socratic dialogue (which proceeds by elenchos toward a conclusion), Chan mondō typically turns on a single exchange in which the master's response cuts through the student's question rather than answering it. The student asks expecting an answer within the conceptual frame the question opens; the master's response refuses the frame entirely. The point is not the transmission of information but the occasion of direct insight — the student is meant to see through the question, not to receive an answer to it.

gloss: face-to-face transmission — the direct, intimate passing of dharma from master to disciple in physical co-presence; the mode of transmission Dōgen considered essential to authentic lineage
notes: A Chan compound given its most consequential articulation by Dōgen, who insisted that face-to-face transmission was the only legitimate mode of dharma succession. Dōgen's emphasis was partly polemical: against schools that accepted transmission through texts, dreams, or visionary encounters, he argued that the physical co-presence of master and disciple was non-negotiable. The Shōbōgenzō fascicle 'Menju' elaborates the claim in detail. The doctrinal stake is that what is transmitted in dharma succession is not information (which could be conveyed by text) but the awakened mind itself (which can only be recognized in the living encounter between two persons). This makes 面授 not merely an institutional preference but a doctrinal requirement: the structure of mind-to-mind transmission demands face-to-face encounter.

gloss: dharma transmission — formal recognition of a disciple as a dharma heir, continuing the lineage from Śākyamuni Buddha through the Indian and Chinese patriarchs to the present teacher
notes: A Chan/Zen institutional concept without a direct Sanskrit antecedent. Dharma transmission is the mechanism by which the Chan/Zen tradition maintains its self-understanding as an unbroken lineage from the historical Buddha. The transmission is not the passing of a body of doctrine but the master's formal recognition that the disciple has attained authentic realization and is qualified to teach in their own right. The institutional form varies between lineages: Rinzai transmission is typically associated with the completion of the formal koan curriculum; Sōtō transmission involves a formal ceremony of document-copying and acknowledgment. Dōgen placed extreme emphasis on 面授 (menju, face-to-face transmission), insisting that authentic lineage requires the physical co-presence of master and disciple.

gloss: the mind of awakening — the aspiration to attain complete Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings; the essential first step of the Mahāyāna path
notes: From Sanskrit bodhi (awakening) + citta (mind). Bodhicitta is the aspiration that distinguishes the Mahāyāna path from the Hīnayāna: the practitioner seeks awakening not for personal liberation alone but for the benefit of all sentient beings. East Asian Buddhism renders the concept as 菩提心 (bodaishin, the awakening-mind), and the compound 発菩提心 (hotsu bodaishin, arousing the awakening-mind) names the first moment at which this aspiration arises. Dōgen treats hotsu bodaishin as the essential foundation of the Buddhist path in the Shōbōgenzō fascicle of the same name, emphasizing that the aspiration is not a feeling or a resolve but the first functional expression of the practice-realization unity: the aspiration to awaken is already itself an expression of the awakening it seeks.

gloss: negotiating the Way — wholehearted engagement in practice; the active, full-bodied exertion of the practitioner in the work of the Buddhist path
notes: The compound 弁道 appears in earlier Chan vocabulary but takes its most consequential articulation in Dōgen's Bendōwa (弁道話, 'A Talk on Negotiating the Way'), the foundational essay of his teaching career. The 弁 is doing precise work: it names practice not as following instructions or performing a technique but as actively negotiating — engaging with, working through, and throwing oneself into the Way. The word 'negotiate' is closer to the original sense than 'practice' alone: the Way is not something one merely follows but something one engages with as a counterpart, something that responds to the practitioner's exertion in ways that cannot be fully predicted. The essay Bendōwa is the primary text in which Dōgen introduces his major doctrinal categories: 修証一等, 自受用三昧, the universality of zazen, the superiority of shikantaza.

gloss: continuous practice — the sustained, ceaseless activity of the Buddhist Way; practice conceived not as episodic effort but as an unbroken circle that sustains itself across moments, lives, and the generations of the lineage
notes: A Chinese compound reactivated with new force in Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō, where it is the subject of a major two-part fascicle ('Gyōji'). The term is present in earlier Chan literature but Dōgen gives it a distinctive reading: 行持 names not the practitioner's effort to practice continuously but the Way's own continuous activity expressed through the practitioner. The practice sustains itself — the practitioner participates in rather than generates the continuity. This reading supports the related concept of 行持道環 (gyōji dōkan, the circle of the Way in continuous practice), in which the practice-realization relationship is figured as a self-sustaining circle rather than a linear path from practice to result.

gloss: self-receiving and self-employing samādhi — Dōgen's term from the Bendōwa for zazen as a meditative absorption that receives itself from itself and employs itself in itself, requiring no external occasion or further purpose to be complete
notes: A signature Dōgen formulation built from the Sanskrit-derived 三昧 (samādhi) and the philosophical pair 自受 (self-receiving) and 自用 (self-employing). The compound describes zazen as a samādhi whose source, content, and purpose are all internal to the practice itself: the practice receives itself from itself, employs itself in itself, and serves no further goal because it is already the activity any further goal would name. The doctrinal stake is the same as 修証一等 (oneness of practice and realization): if practice is the activity of awakening rather than a means to it, then the samādhi of practice cannot be received from outside or employed for some further purpose, because there is no outside and no further purpose. The Bendōwa essay introduces the term and elaborates its significance.

gloss: the rain retreat — the intensive communal training period of three months traditionally observed during the South Asian monsoon, in which monks ceased traveling and gathered for sustained practice; the East Asian and Japanese descendants of this institution
notes: The Sanskrit varṣā (rain) names the original institutional context: during the Indian monsoon (roughly June to September) monks could not travel without damaging crops and ground-dwelling life, so they gathered at fixed locations for sustained practice. This pragmatic accommodation became one of the most stable institutions of Buddhist monasticism and was carried throughout the Buddhist world. East Asian Buddhism preserved the institution as 安居 (Chinese ānjū, Japanese ango), though the seasonal alignment shifted to fit local climate — Japanese ango is often held in summer (夏安居) but also exists as a winter retreat (雪安居). In Chan/Zen monasteries the period is the principal occasion for sustained communal practice and ceremonial markers like the appointment of the shuso (head student) and the hossenshiki (dharma combat ceremony) at its conclusion.

gloss: meditative absorption — the unified, one-pointed concentration in which mind and object converge into a single field of awareness; one of the foundational categories of Buddhist meditation psychology
notes: From the Sanskrit roots sam- (together) and ā-dhā (to place), literally the placing-together that constitutes unified attention. Samādhi is one of the three pillars of the Buddhist path in early formulations (śīla, samādhi, prajñā — ethics, concentration, wisdom) and is analyzed in detail in Abhidharma psychology as a class of meditative attainments with internal taxonomy. East Asian Buddhism inherits the Sanskrit term phonetically as 三昧 (Chinese sānmèi, Japanese zanmai) and uses the compound for both the technical concentration of meditation and the broader sense of complete absorption in any activity. In Chan/Zen contexts, samādhi is understood not as a special state to be achieved but as the natural mode of awareness that becomes available when grasping ceases — closer to the Sōtō understanding of zazen as the activity of awakening than to the gradualist conception of samādhi as a stage on a progressive path.

gloss: gathering the mind — an intensive meditation retreat, typically five to seven days, of near-continuous zazen with all monastic activities organized to support the singleness of practice
notes: A specifically Chan/Zen monastic institution rather than a translation from Sanskrit. Sesshin retreats developed within the Chan tradition as periods of concentrated practice during which the regular monastic schedule intensifies: zazen sessions extend, walking meditation, formal meals, and brief work periods are tightly scheduled, sleep is reduced, and casual conversation is suspended. The structure is designed so that all the conditions of monastic life converge to support the gathering of the mind into the unified attention that practice requires. In contemporary Japanese and Western Zen practice, sesshin remains the principal occasion for sustained intensive practice, typically held several times a year in established monasteries and Zen centers.

gloss: walking meditation — slow, mindful walking practiced between periods of seated zazen, in which the activity of walking is engaged with the same quality of attention as the activity of sitting
notes: The Sanskrit antecedent is caṅkrama, the walking meditation practiced in the early Buddhist forest tradition and described in the Pali canon. The Chinese 経行 (jīngxíng) preserves the practice in monastic East Asian Buddhism and is integral to Chan/Zen monastic schedules: between periods of zazen, monks walk slowly in single file around the meditation hall or along a designated path, maintaining the same quality of embodied attention they bring to sitting. The doctrinal point is that practice is not confined to the seated posture — the activity of walking, engaged with the same quality of presence, is itself the practice. This is consistent with the Sōtō principle that practice is the activity of awakening rather than a means to it.

gloss: just sitting — Dōgen's name for objectless, technique-free meditation in which the activity of sitting is itself the entire practice, with no further goal, no koan, no breath count, and no aim beyond the sitting that is happening
notes: A specifically Sōtō term, formed from the Chinese 只管 (single-mindedly, exclusively) and 打坐 (doing sitting). Dōgen learned the practice from his Chinese teacher Tiantong Rujing (Tendō Nyojō) at Mt. Tendō and made it the central practice of the Sōtō tradition he founded in Japan. The doctrinal point of shikantaza is the refusal of any framework that would treat zazen as a technique aimed at producing some other state. There is nothing to achieve through sitting because sitting is itself the activity of awakening (修証一等, oneness of practice and realization). The practice is therefore not the application of a method but the dropping of all methods, and what remains is simply the sitting that practice consists in. Shikantaza is often misread as 'sitting and doing nothing' or as 'mindfulness of sitting,' both of which import precisely the goal-orientation it refuses.

gloss: meditative absorption — the focused concentration of mind in sustained meditation; the practice of structured contemplation that all Buddhist traditions inherit from the pre-Buddhist śramaṇa milieu
notes: The Sanskrit dhyāna names a specific class of meditative attainments analyzed in detail in early Buddhist psychology — the four rūpa-jhānas of form-meditation and the four arūpa-jhānas of formless meditation. East Asian Buddhism inherited this analysis but the technical taxonomy is rarely the foreground of Chan/Zen practice; the term 禅 became attached to the school precisely because the school took meditation as its defining activity rather than as one technical category among others. The phonetic transliteration 禅 (chán → zen) preserves the Sanskrit sound while abandoning most of the technical taxonomic baggage, which is doctrinally fitting: Chan/Zen is interested in dhyāna as the activity through which awakening is occasioned, not as a graduated map of meditative states to be achieved sequentially.

gloss: impermanence-is-Buddha-nature — Dōgen's radical formulation in the Shōbōgenzō 'Busshō' fascicle, identifying impermanence (the foundational mark of all conditioned phenomena) with Buddha-nature itself, dissolving the apparent opposition between the Three Dharma Seals and Tathāgatagarbha doctrine
notes: Not a translation from Sanskrit but a Dōgen formulation built from existing Buddhist vocabulary. The doctrinal stake is significant. The Three Dharma Seals identify all conditioned things as impermanent (諸行無常); Tathāgatagarbha and certain Mahāyāna sutras affirm Buddha-nature as constant (常). These two claims have generated centuries of doctrinal exegesis trying to reconcile them. Dōgen's move in the 'Busshō' fascicle is to refuse the reconciliation by collapsing the opposition: impermanence is not the obstacle to Buddha-nature but is Buddha-nature, and the constancy attributed to Buddha-nature must be understood not as the absence of change but as the very mode in which change occurs. The formulation is philosophically dense and has been the subject of extensive scholarship in modern Sōtō studies.

gloss: original mind — the inherently pure, undefiled mind prior to the arising of delusion; in Chan/Zen vocabulary the mode of mind that is to be recognized rather than achieved
notes: A Chinese-Japanese formulation rather than a translation of a single Sanskrit term. The compound 本心 carries the structural sense of 本 (root, origin, originally) applied to 心 (heart-mind): the mind in its original condition, prior to and beneath the elaborations of delusion. The Platform Sutra uses the term centrally — 不識本心、学法無益 (not recognizing the original mind, learning the dharma is useless) — as the foundational claim of Chan/Zen practice. The doctrinal point is that the original mind is not a memory of a former state or a reachable future state but the present mind seen as it actually is, prior to the constructions that ordinarily cover it over.

gloss: Buddha-mind — the awakened mind, equivalent in function to Buddha-nature but emphasizing the cognitive-affective register; the mind of an awakened being, identified by Chan/Zen with the practitioner's own mind when free of obstruction
notes: The compound 仏心 (Chinese fóxīn, Japanese busshin) translates and elaborates the Sanskrit buddha-citta in a register that emphasizes the heart-mind aspect of awakening over the abstract notion of Buddha-nature (仏性). The Chan/Zen tradition is sometimes called 仏心宗 (busshinshū, the Buddha-mind school), reflecting the school's foundational claim that what is transmitted from master to disciple is not a doctrine but the awakened mind itself, recognized as already present in the disciple. The compound foregrounds the same identification that 即心是仏 makes more concentrated: there is no Buddha apart from the mind, and no mind apart from Buddha when ordinary discriminating activity is not generating the appearance of separation.

term: píngcháng xīn shì dào / byōjōshin kore dō
gloss: ordinary mind is the Way — Mazu Daoyi's formulation that the everyday, unexceptional functioning of mind is itself the Way of practice and awakening, not a stepping stone toward something more exalted
notes: Attributed to Mazu Daoyi, the same Tang Chan master associated with 即心是仏. The formula appears most famously in Mumonkan Case 19, where Nansen (Nanquan Puyuan) gives it to his student Jōshū (Zhaozhou Congshen) — though the formulation is older and is associated with the broader Hongzhou school. The doctrinal point is to refuse the gradualist temptation to treat practice as the cultivation of an extraordinary mind that does not yet exist. The mind that practice engages is the ordinary mind one already has — the only mind there is — and the Way is what that ordinary mind does when it is not generating obstructions. The formula is often misread as a quietist license to do nothing special; the koan record is consistently careful to refuse this reading.

term: jí xīn shì fó / sokushin zebutsu
gloss: this very mind is Buddha — Mazu Daoyi's cardinal Chan formula asserting that the presently functioning mind is itself Buddhahood, with no gap, no mediation, and no future state to be reached
notes: Attributed to Mazu Daoyi (709–788), the Tang-dynasty Chan master whose teaching shaped the Hongzhou school and through it the entire later Chan/Zen tradition. The formula appears in the Mumonkan (Gateless Gate) Case 30 and in the Blue Cliff Record Case 73. Mazu's biography records that he later modified the formula to 非心非仏 (not mind, not Buddha) when he saw students clinging to 即心是仏 as a doctrinal position to be held — the modification preserves the doctrinal point while breaking the attachment to its formulation. The two formulas together model the characteristic Chan refusal to let any teaching become a fixed position the practitioner can rest in.

gloss: body-mind as one — the doctrinal claim that the lived body and the heart-mind are not two separable entities but a single field of embodied experience, foundational to Dōgen's account of zazen as the activity of the whole person
notes: Not directly a translation from Sanskrit. The phrase crystallizes a position with deep roots in Mahāyāna nondualism but takes its specifically Japanese articulation in Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō, where the unity of body and mind is repeatedly affirmed against any framing that would treat practice as a mental discipline conducted in a separable body. The doctrinal stake is significant: if body and mind are one, then zazen is not the mind sitting in a body but the whole embodied person engaging in a single integrated activity, and the gradualist temptation to treat the body as the obstacle to mental clarity is dissolved at its root.

gloss: own-nature, inherent self-existence — the doctrinally contested notion that a thing has an independent, intrinsic essence that constitutes it apart from its causes and relations
notes: The central target of Madhyamaka critique. Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā argues at length that nothing has svabhāva, because everything arises dependently on causes and conditions, and what arises dependently cannot also exist independently. The Chinese rendering 自性 preserves the structure: 自 (self) + 性 (nature). The doctrinal tension is that East Asian Tathāgatagarbha-influenced traditions sometimes use 自性 positively — to refer to one's original Buddha-nature as 'self-nature' — creating an apparent collision with Madhyamaka's denial. Careful Chan/Zen commentators distinguish two senses: the svabhāva that Madhyamaka denies (inherent independent essence) and the 自性 that Chan affirms (the nature of mind that is to be seen, which is itself empty of svabhāva in the Madhyamaka sense). The terminological collision is real and has generated centuries of doctrinal exegesis.

gloss: the nature of dharmas — the intrinsic, defining character of phenomena; what dharmas are in themselves prior to any conceptual or practical sorting
notes: An abstract noun formed from dharma, parallel in formation to tathatā (suchness) from tathā (thus). Dharmatā names the nature of phenomena considered as a whole — what they share by virtue of being phenomena at all. In Madhyamaka the answer to 'what is the nature of dharmas?' is emptiness (śūnyatā): dharmas have no inherent self-nature, and that absence is their dharmatā. The Chinese rendering 法性 (fǎxìng, hosshō) preserves the abstract structure but lets later doctrinal traditions read it in different ways — sometimes as the bare absence Madhyamaka points at, sometimes as a positive ground in Tathāgatagarbha-influenced readings. Dōgen devotes a Shōbōgenzō fascicle to 法性, treating it as a dynamic and constantly self-manifesting reality rather than a static metaphysical substrate.

gloss: suchness, thusness — the true nature of reality just as it is, prior to and beyond all conceptual elaboration; the way things are when not overlaid by the discriminating activity of mind
notes: Central term of Yogācāra and Madhyamaka thought, derived from the simple Sanskrit demonstrative tathā ('thus, in this way'). Tathatā names not a special metaphysical substance but the bare fact of things being as they are — a deflationary rather than inflationary concept. The Awakening of Faith treatise treats tathatā as the absolute ground; later East Asian elaborations sometimes hypostatize it as a metaphysical reality, against which the Madhyamaka strain of the tradition consistently warns. The Chinese rendering 真如 doubles the emphasis with 真 (true) — the true thusness, as opposed to a mistaken or partial one. The compound is doctrinally inseparable from the epithet 如来 (Tathāgata, 'thus-come'), which makes the same word the name of a Buddha.

gloss: no-mind — awareness free from fixation, clinging, and the discriminating self-reference of the ordinary ego; the unobstructed functioning of consciousness when it is not grasping at its own contents
notes: A Chan Chinese formulation rather than a translation from Sanskrit, though it has affinities with the Sanskrit acitta and with the Mādhyamika critique of clinging. The term enters Chan vocabulary by the Tang period and becomes central to the Linji/Rinzai pedagogical tradition. The 'no' of 無心 does not mean the absence of consciousness — that would be 不覚 (un-wakefulness) or simple unconsciousness — but the absence of the grasping, fixating activity by which the ordinary mind constructs an objectified self separate from its experience. 無心 as a positive term names the unobstructed flow that is uncovered when this construction stops. The term has substantial life outside Buddhist texts as well: in Japanese aesthetics and the martial arts traditions of the Tokugawa period (kendō, kyūdō, sadō, shodō), 無心 names the state of skilled action in which technique has become so internalized that conscious deliberation no longer interferes.

gloss: Buddha-nature; the Buddha-element or womb of the Tathāgata — the doctrine that all sentient beings possess (or are) the intrinsic nature of awakening, the seed or substrate of Buddhahood
notes: Two distinct but overlapping Sanskrit terms — buddha-dhātu (the Buddha-element) and tathāgatagarbha (the womb or embryo of the Tathāgata) — converge in the East Asian rendering 仏性 (Chinese fóxìng, Japanese busshō). The doctrine is elaborated in scriptures like the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra, the Śrīmālādevī Sūtra, and most importantly the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, which contains the foundational claim that all sentient beings have Buddha-nature (一切衆生悉有仏性). Dōgen's radical rereading in the Shōbōgenzō 'Busshō' fascicle proposes that this should be read not as a possession relation ('all beings have Buddha-nature') but as an identity ('all being is Buddha-nature') — a syntactic reanalysis with major doctrinal consequences.

gloss: Buddhahood — the attained condition of being a fully awakened one; the ultimate horizon of Buddhist soteriology, in Mahāyāna understood as the goal of the bodhisattva path
notes: Sanskrit buddhatva is the abstract noun formed from buddha (awakened one); buddha-prāpti is the action of attaining Buddhahood. East Asian Buddhism renders this through the verbal compound 成仏 (jōbutsu), in which the verb of becoming (成) is doing the load-bearing work. The Chan/Zen claim that 成仏 is not the production of something new but the manifestation of what one already is — 見性成仏, seeing one's nature is becoming Buddha — works on the Chinese-Japanese verbal structure in a way that Sanskrit's nominal abstraction does not directly invite. The doctrine of universal Buddhahood (一切衆生悉有仏性) is the necessary condition for this reading.

gloss: the great death — the figural ego-death that must precede genuine awakening; the complete dissolution of the ordinary subject-object structure of consciousness, after which one is 'born into the great life' of awakening
notes: Not a translation from Sanskrit but a Chan Chinese formulation that crystallized in the Linji/Rinzai lineage. The compound is paired structurally with 大悟 (great awakening): the great death is what 大悟 requires as its precondition. The phrase 大死一番、絶後再蘇 (great death one time, then revival after the cutting-off) is a stock Chan formulation describing the sequence: a complete cessation of the discriminating self, followed by a re-emergence into a transformed mode of functioning. The figural language of death is doing precise doctrinal work: it names the kind of transformation awakening requires by analogy to the only experience of total cessation ordinary life provides.

gloss: acquired or initiated enlightenment — awakening as it arrives for a particular practitioner at a particular time, the recognition of what 本覚 (hongaku) names as always-already-the-case
notes: Like 本覚, a Chinese-Japanese doctrinal formation rooted in the Awakening of Faith. The Tendai tradition elaborated 始覚 as the necessary counterpart of 本覚: without 始覚, 本覚 would be a metaphysical claim with no practical purchase; without 本覚, 始覚 would be the production of something new rather than the recognition of what is. The two terms together describe a single relationship — they are not competing accounts of awakening but two perspectives on one event. Dōgen's 修証一等 (oneness of practice and realization) can be read as a way of holding both moments together without privileging either.

gloss: original enlightenment — the doctrine that all sentient beings are intrinsically and originally awakened, with practice and acquired enlightenment (始覚) understood as the recognition rather than the production of what is always already the case
notes: Not directly a translation from Sanskrit but a Chinese-Japanese doctrinal formation rooted in the Awakening of Faith (大乗起信論, Dasheng qixin lun), a sixth-century treatise of disputed authorship that became foundational for East Asian Buddhism. Hongaku thought reaches its most elaborated form in medieval Japanese Tendai, where it develops into a systematic theology of intrinsic awakening that influenced all subsequent Japanese Buddhism — the Pure Land schools, Zen, and Nichiren. Dōgen's relationship to hongaku is complex and central: he interrogates its potential to collapse into a quietism that denies the necessity of practice, while himself developing a position that practice is not separate from the original enlightenment it might seem to seek.

gloss: gradual awakening — the Northern school's doctrine that genuine enlightenment is reached through progressive purification, sustained practice, and the stage-by-stage removal of defilements rather than through a single instantaneous breakthrough
notes: The structural counterpart to 頓悟 (dùnwù). The Platform Sutra polemically associates 漸悟 with Shenxiu and the Northern school, framing it as inferior to Huineng's sudden teaching. Modern scholarship has rehabilitated the so-called Northern school: what was caricatured as a doctrine of grinding incremental purification was in fact a sophisticated practice tradition that did not deny the suddenness of recognition but emphasized the cultivation needed to occasion and stabilize it. The 頓漸 distinction is best read as a difference of pedagogical emphasis within Chan, not as a clean opposition between awakening and non-awakening.

gloss: sudden awakening — the Southern school's doctrine that genuine enlightenment arrives as an instantaneous, structurally complete breakthrough rather than through gradual accumulation of insight
notes: A Chinese Buddhist doctrinal formation with no direct Sanskrit antecedent — the sudden/gradual (頓漸, dùnjiàn) distinction is a controversy internal to Tang-dynasty Chan, not a translation of an Indian debate. The Platform Sutra presents Huineng's teaching as sudden (頓) against Shenxiu's gradual (漸) approach. The doctrinal claim of 頓悟 is not merely that awakening is fast but that it is structurally instantaneous — there is no partial or incomplete awakening that then completes itself over time. The awakening either sees through completely (大悟, great awakening) or has not yet arrived. This raises the pedagogical question of what practice is for if awakening cannot be accumulated: the Chan answer is that practice removes the obscurations preventing recognition of what is already fully present.

gloss: dharma combat ceremony — the formal ritual exchange of Zen questions and answers in which the shuso (head seat) faces the assembly and responds to their challenges, marking the culmination of a practice period and the shuso's emergence as a teacher in training
notes: Not a translation from Sanskrit but a Chan/Zen monastic institution developed in Song-dynasty China and transmitted to Japan in the Kamakura period. The ceremony presents the shuso publicly for the first time as a respondent rather than a student: the shuso takes the teacher's seat, and members of the assembly rise in turn to pose dharma questions. The shuso must answer each challenge in real time and in the high-stakes register of Zen encounter language — the exchange is neither an examination in the academic sense nor an ordinary mondō but something between them, conducted under the sign of ritual combat. The figure of 戦 (combat) is not a softened metaphor: the ceremony preserves the Chan insistence that dharma encounter is a real contest of understanding, with the ritual form protecting and intensifying rather than diluting the stakes. Dōgen's Eihei Shingi preserves detailed instructions for the ceremony, and hossenshiki remains a live institution in both Sōtō and Rinzai training today.

gloss: within the room — the spatial and institutional figure for the esoteric, lineage-internal teaching held in the master's private chamber; by extension the body of transmitted koan responses and encounter answers that circulate only within a lineage's dokusan chamber
notes: A Chan/Zen institutional concept with no direct Sanskrit antecedent. The literal sense is simply 'inside the room' — specifically the room in which dokusan (private interview) is conducted. The specialized technical sense is more consequential: shitsunai denotes the entire body of transmitted koan responses, capping phrases, and encounter formulations held within a particular lineage, passed only from teacher to student in the privacy of the dokusan chamber and never published. In the Rinzai koan curriculum the shitsunai is a living oral and gestural tradition distinct from the printed koan collections (Gateless Gate, Blue Cliff Record): the printed collections preserve the main cases, but the shitsunai preserves the lineage's specific transmitted responses to each case — the answers the student must present in dokusan to pass the koan. The spatial figure is doctrinally load-bearing: what is shitsunai cannot be made public without ceasing to be shitsunai. The distinction between public teishō and private shitsunai instruction structures the Rinzai transmission system at every level.

gloss: public case — a recorded encounter between master and student (or master and master) from the Chan ancestors, taken as a precedent-setting case and used as an object of meditative inquiry; the literary and pedagogical genre through which the Chan tradition transmits its understanding of what awakening is
notes: Originally a term of Tang-dynasty Chinese magistrate's vocabulary: 公案 was the magistrate's public docket, the case-file recording a precedent-setting judgment. Chan teachers recruited the term in the late Tang and early Song to name the recorded encounters of the ancestors, exploiting the juridical figure's precise structure: a case once decided is a precedent available to all later cases, and the student approaches the ancestor's response as a living precedent to meet rather than as a puzzle to solve or an opinion to weigh. The systematic use of 公案 as meditation objects — kanhua or koan-introspecting Zen — is associated with Dahui Zonggao (1089–1163) in the Linji lineage, who developed the method of concentrating on the 話頭 (huàtóu, critical phrase) of a case rather than analyzing the case as a whole. The koan literature comprises both compilations (Gateless Gate, Blue Cliff Record, Book of Serenity) and the lineage-internal shitsunai traditions preserving each lineage's transmitted responses. The doctrinal stake is that the koan is not a problem to solve but a precedent to enact — the student must demonstrate the ancestor's understanding in the student's own body and voice, not describe it.

gloss: head of the word — the single critical phrase or word at the decisive point of a koan utterance, isolated from the full case and held in meditative awareness as the focal point of concentrated inquiry; the technical core of Dahui Zonggao's kanhua method
notes: A Chan term systematized by Dahui Zonggao (1089–1163) in the Linji lineage as a reform of koan practice. Dahui's innovation was to distinguish the full 話 (the entire recorded case) from its 頭 (its head, its critical point) and to instruct practitioners to concentrate on the 頭 alone rather than analyzing the full case. For Zhaozhou's famous dog-Buddha-nature koan, the 話頭 is the bare 無 (Ch. wú, no) — not the question that precedes it or the commentary that surrounds it but the single word at which the exchange concentrates its force. The practitioner holds this critical phrase in awareness without interpretation, without seeking an answer, allowing it to function as a concentrated focal point that the discriminating mind cannot dissolve. Dahui's method was partly polemical: he framed it against what he called 'silent illumination' Zen (黙照禅, attributed to Hongzhi Zhengjue and the Caodong/Sōtō lineage), arguing that sitting without an object gave the dull mind nothing to work against. The kanhua/watō method became the characteristic practice of Song-dynasty Linji Chan and was transmitted to Japan as the core of the Rinzai curriculum. Modern Korean Seon also centers on hwadu (the Korean reading of 話頭) practice as the dominant meditation method.

gloss: koan-introspecting Chan — the meditation method systematized by Dahui Zonggao in which the practitioner sustains concentrated inward looking at the critical phrase (話頭) of a koan as the object of non-discursive inquiry, the characteristic practice of the Linji/Rinzai lineage from the Song dynasty onward
notes: Kànhuà chán is the meditative method in which the practitioner 'looks at' (看) a critical phrase or 'head of the word' (話頭) extracted from a koan and holds it in concentrated awareness as the sustained object of inquiry. Dahui Zonggao (1089–1163) systematized the method in the Linji lineage during the Song dynasty, partly as a reform of older koan practices that had grown too literary and partly in polemical opposition to the Caodong lineage's 'silent illumination' (mòzhào chán, 黙照禅). Dahui's argument against silent illumination was that objectless sitting left the dull practitioner with nothing to work against and risked collapsing into mere torpor; the 話頭 provided a concentrated focal point that the discriminating mind could neither resolve by analysis nor escape by inattention. Kànhuà chán became the dominant pedagogy of Song-dynasty Linji Chan and was transmitted to Japan through Eisai and subsequent Rinzai masters, where it remains the backbone of Japanese kōan practice. Modern Korean Seon also centers on hwadu (the Korean reading of 話頭) practice as its principal meditation method. The character 看 (to look at, to watch with sustained attention) is doctrinally precise: the practitioner is instructed to 'look at' the phrase rather than to 'think about' it, because looking can be sustained without generating content while thinking cannot.

gloss: silent illumination Chan — the Caodong/Sōtō meditative mode of objectless sitting in which silence (the suspension of discursive activity) and illumination (the luminous clarity of awareness) are held as the two inseparable aspects of a single zazen, articulated classically by Hongzhi Zhengjue and radicalized by Dōgen as shikantaza
notes: Mòzhào chán is the characteristic practice and doctrinal position of the Caodong lineage during the Song dynasty, articulated most fully by Hongzhi Zhengjue (1091–1157) in the short verse-inscription 黙照銘 (Silent Illumination Inscription). The term names the pairing of two aspects of zazen that the Caodong tradition insists are not successive stages or alternating modes but one activity seen from two sides: 黙 (silence) as the suspension of discursive proliferation, the stilling of the mind's habit of producing internal commentary; 照 (illumination) as the luminous clarity of awareness that rests in and as that silence, the aspect under which phenomena are seen as they are without interpretive overlay. The crucial claim is that these two are not separable — the silence is not preparatory to illumination, and the illumination is not a cognitive act added onto silence — and Hongzhi's inscription is constructed to hold this insistence in every line. Dahui Zonggao, in the Linji lineage, attacked 'silent illumination' as a euphemism for mere torpor and advanced kànhuà chán (koan-introspecting Chan) as a corrective. The polemic hardened the Linji/Rinzai and Caodong/Sōtō positions into their classical opposition, but Hongzhi's own writings are more subtle than Dahui's caricature admits: mozhao is not mental blankness but the precise, demanding meeting of stillness and clear awareness. Dōgen inherits this line directly — his reception of Tiantong Rujing's teaching in the Caodong lineage is explicitly within the mozhao tradition — and radicalizes it as shikantaza (只管打坐, just sitting) and as the unity-formula of practice-realization (修証一等).

gloss: capping phrase — a short phrase, verse, or literary allusion appended to a recorded koan case as the commentator's or student's compressed demonstration of insight into the case, functioning by fit rather than by explanation
notes: A Chan/Zen pedagogical and literary institution with no direct Sanskrit antecedent. A 着語 is a short phrase — sometimes a single line of classical Chinese poetry, sometimes a fragment of a Confucian or Daoist text, sometimes a line drawn from older Chan literature, sometimes the commentator's own composition — appended to a recorded koan case to express the commentator's understanding of it. The capping phrase does not explain the case; it responds to it in kind, enacting insight rather than describing it. The governing figure is precise: the phrase 'attaches' (着) to the case by fitting it, and a phrase that does not fit is simply a phrase. In the Rinzai koan curriculum the student is required to present capping phrases as part of passing a case: after demonstrating the main response, the student offers one or more phrases drawn from an internalized repertoire catalogued in phrase books such as the Zenrin Kushū (禅林句集), and the teacher judges whether the phrases fit. The Blue Cliff Record's commentarial layers — Xuedou Chongxian's verse commentaries (頌古) and Yuanwu Keqin's pointers, interlinear capping comments, and prose commentaries — are the most celebrated literary instance of the genre. 着語 (jakugo, Ch. zhuóyǔ) and 下語 (agyo, Ch. xiàyǔ) are often treated as synonyms, though some traditions distinguish 着語 as the commentator's authoritative capping phrase and 下語 as the student's offered attempt.

gloss: appended words — a short phrase set down beside a koan case as a compressed response to it, roughly synonymous with 着語 (jakugo / zhuoyu) but often specifically denoting the student's offered phrase in dokusan rather than the commentator's authoritative capping
notes: 着語 (jakugo) and 下語 (agyo) are overlapping terms in the Chan/Zen commentarial vocabulary, both naming short phrases appended to a koan case as a compressed response. The most common distinction treats 着語 as the authoritative capping phrase offered by a master or recognized commentator — Xuedou Chongxian, Yuanwu Keqin, Wansong Xingxiu — and 下語 as the phrase the student sets down in response during dokusan, an offering to be weighed rather than a precedent to be received. Other accounts treat the two terms as functional synonyms with the distinction turning on context rather than kind, and the boundary is porous across the tradition. Both practices circulate within the Rinzai koan curriculum, which maintains large compilations of standardized phrases (notably the Zenrin Kushū) from which students draw their offerings. The figure of 下 (putting down, setting down) is precise and doctrinally important: the student does not argue for or against the case but sets words down beside it — places them as an offering — and the master weighs whether the words that fell are the ones the case asks for. The parallel with 着 in 着語 is instructive: 着 names the attaching, 下 names the placing; both name modes of offering a phrase to a case without claiming to explain it, and both preserve in ritualized form the older Chan insistence that understanding is demonstrated rather than argued.

gloss: picking up and presenting — a master's commentary that isolates the essential point of a koan case and holds it up for the assembly, expounding it without reducing it to explanation
notes: 拈提 (nentei, Ch. niāntí) names the Chan/Zen commentarial act in which a master selects the critical point of a recorded koan case and presents it to the assembly with commentary. The two characters divide the act precisely: 拈 (to pick up between the fingers, to select delicately from among many) isolates the point; 提 (to lift up, to present, to hold aloft) brings it into view. The compound names not a genre of written commentary but a mode of teaching: the master picks up a case that already exists in the archive — an old exchange between Chan ancestors — and holds up the point within it that the current assembly needs to see. The commentary that accompanies the 拈提 is typically oral and extemporaneous, delivered in the formal setting of a jōdō (ascending the hall) or teishō (formal presentation), and it demonstrates rather than explains: the master's handling of the point is itself the teaching, and a 拈提 that merely paraphrased the case would have failed. The term overlaps with 拈古 (nenko, picking up the old) but is generally distinguished from it: 拈古 names the broader literary genre of selecting an old case and adding commentary (including written commentary and verse), while 拈提 names the specific act of isolating and expounding the essential point, typically in a live teaching context. The distinction is not rigid across the tradition, and some texts use the terms interchangeably.

gloss: picking up the old — the literary genre of selecting an ancient koan case from the archive and adding commentary, the fundamental act underlying the compilation of koan collections
notes: 拈古 (nenko, Ch. niāngǔ) names both a literary genre and a commentarial practice: the act of selecting an ancient Chan case (古, the old) and picking it up (拈) for commentary. The genre is the structural foundation of the koan collection tradition — the Blue Cliff Record, the Gateless Gate, and the Book of Serenity all exist because their compilers engaged in 拈古, selecting old cases and adding layers of commentary. The compound's two characters map the act precisely: 拈 names the selective, delicate taking-up (not a full-handed seizure but a precise pinching between the fingers), and 古 names the temporal location of the material — it is old, ancient, from the founding generations of the Chan lineage. The Chan claim embedded in the compound is that the old cases are not closed archives but living material that must be picked up anew in each generation; the act of 拈古 is what keeps the archive alive. The genre encompasses several sub-forms: prose commentary (as in Yuanwu's prose remarks in the Blue Cliff Record), verse commentary (頌古 juko, as in Xuedou's hundred verses), and the briefer nentei (拈提, picking up and presenting the essential point). Some accounts treat 拈古 as the umbrella genre under which 頌古 and 拈提 are sub-genres; others treat the three as parallel forms. The boundary is historically fluid.

gloss: main case — the core narrative or dialogue of a koan as recorded in a collection, the decided precedent that the student must meet and that the commentarial layers (verse, pointer, capping phrase) all address
notes: 本則 (honsoku, Ch. běnzé) names the core narrative of a koan case as it appears in a koan collection — the recorded exchange, episode, or dialogue that constitutes the case itself, prior to and distinct from the commentarial layers (verse, pointer, prose commentary, capping phrase) that surround it. 本 (root, original, fundamental) marks the case as the foundation of the commentary structure, and 則 (rule, standard, case — used as a counter for koan cases) names the unit of precedent. The compound thus means literally 'the fundamental case' or 'the root standard,' and its function in the architecture of a koan collection is precisely analogous to the case text in a legal record: the 本則 is the decided precedent, and everything else — Xuedou's verse, Yuanwu's pointer, the interlinear capping phrases — is commentary on it. In the Blue Cliff Record the 本則 of each of the hundred cases is presented first, then surrounded by Xuedou's verse (頌古), Yuanwu's pointer (垂示), and Yuanwu's prose commentary. In the Gateless Gate the 本則 is followed by Wumen's commentary and verse. The student working through a koan collection engages the 本則 as the primary object — the commentary may guide or provoke, but the case itself is what must be met. The term is also used as a general designation for 'main text' in other Buddhist commentarial contexts, but its primary home in Japanese and Chinese Buddhist usage is the koan collection genre.

gloss: verse on an old case — poetic commentary composed in response to a recorded koan, the genre in which the commentator demonstrates insight through the creation of a parallel aesthetic object rather than through analysis
notes: 頌古 (juko, Ch. sònggǔ) names the genre of verse commentary on koan cases — a poem composed in response to a recorded Chan dialogue or episode, functioning not as an explanation of the case but as a parallel expression of its insight in a different register. The two characters divide the form: 頌 (verse, hymn, gāthā — a formal poetic composition) names the literary form, and 古 (old, ancient) names the temporal location of the material being versified. The genre's supreme practitioner is Xuedou Chongxian (雪竇重顕, 980–1052), whose hundred verses on selected koan cases became the textual nucleus around which Yuanwu Keqin built the Blue Cliff Record. Xuedou's verses are not explanations — they do not tell the reader what the case means or what the correct response is — but poetic compositions that stand alongside the case as aesthetic companions, responding to its register with a verse that matches its resonance. The genre requires both deep realization of the case and high literary skill, and the tradition has always recognized the combination as rare. After Xuedou, the most celebrated 頌古 practitioner is Hongzhi Zhengjue (1091–1157), whose hundred verses on koan cases were later incorporated by Wansong Xingxiu into the Book of Serenity (從容録). The verse commentary tradition is one of the highest literary achievements of the Chan/Zen tradition, and it preserves the fundamental Chan insight that understanding is demonstrated rather than argued — the verse shows what the case is doing by doing something alongside it in the register of poetry.

gloss: introductory pointer — the commentator's prefatory remarks that hang down over a koan case before the student meets the case directly, a commentarial layer specific to the Blue Cliff Record and related Song-dynasty anthologies
notes: 垂示 (suiji, Ch. chuíshì) names the Chan commentarial genre of the prefatory pointer — a short prose remark by the commentator that is placed before the main case (本則) in a koan anthology and orients the reader without explaining the case. The compound's two characters specify the action: 垂 (to hang down, to bestow, to suspend something downward from a higher to a lower position) names the gesture, and 示 (to show, to display, to make manifest — with the altar origin of the character still active as a semantic residue) names the act. The commentator hangs his remarks down over the case in the manner of something suspended above it, and the reader approaches the case from beneath this overhang. The genre's locus classicus is the Blue Cliff Record (碧巌録), where Yuanwu Keqin (圜悟克勤, 1063–1135) prefaces each of the hundred cases with a 垂示 that performs several rhetorical functions at once: it alerts the reader that the case being presented is dangerous territory, it frames the case's stakes in a register higher than the case itself, and it sometimes issues a direct challenge to the reader before the case has even begun. The 垂示 is not an introduction in the explanatory sense; it does not tell the reader what the case will mean or what the correct response will be. It is closer to a ceremonial opening — a hand raised above the case, suspending something in the air before the case begins. In the Blue Cliff Record's layered architecture the 垂示 sits at the head of each entry, followed by the main case (本則), Xuedou's verse (頌古), Yuanwu's pointer on the verse, Yuanwu's prose commentary, and the interlinear capping phrases. The 垂示 is the first thing the reader encounters and often the last thing the commentator writes — it is composed looking back on the case and its commentary as a whole, and it condenses the commentator's view of the case's stakes into a brief, often cryptic opening gesture. Not every koan collection uses the 垂示 as a structural element: the Gateless Gate (無門関) omits it entirely, and this difference is structurally significant — the Gateless Gate presents each case cold, trusting the student to meet it without prefatory overhang, while the Blue Cliff Record stages each case within an elaborate commentarial architecture in which the 垂示 is the opening layer.

gloss: the Chan shout — a master's sharp vocal cry used as a teaching device to interrupt conceptual proliferation at the moment of arising, emblematic of the Linji/Rinzai lineage
notes: 喝 (katsu, Ch. hè) names the sharp vocal cry used by Chan masters as a direct, non-discursive teaching device. In classical Chinese the character names any angry or scolding shout, but its Chan technical use specializes it into a precise instrument: a sudden explosive vocalization deployed at the exact moment the student is forming a conceptual response, cutting the formation of the thought before it can stabilize into discourse. The figure inseparable from 喝 is Linji Yixuan (臨済義玄, d. 866), the founder of the Linji lineage. Linji is recorded in the Record of Linji (臨済録) as using the shout so frequently and so variously that his disciple Sansheng Huiran asked him to systematize the practice, and Linji responded with the so-called 臨済四喝 — Linji's four shouts. The four are distinguished by function: one is like the treasure-sword of the Vajra king (金剛王宝剣), one is like a golden-haired lion crouching on the ground (踞地獅子), one is like a weed-probing pole with a shadow-grass on it (探竿影草), and the fourth does not function as a shout (不作一喝用). The taxonomy insists that the shout is not a single undifferentiated gesture but a precise pedagogical instrument whose value depends on the exact calibration of its deployment. The doctrinal work the shout performs is to operate at a level prior to discursive thought: it is not an argument, not a rebuke, not an expression of emotion, but a vocal event that occupies the space where the student's thought would have formed, preventing the formation and in the prevention transmitting the teaching. In the later tradition 喝 is paired with 棒 (bō, the staff) as 棒喝 — the staff-and-shout complex — naming the direct, non-discursive pedagogy that defines the Rinzai/Linji lineage's self-understanding. The term enters Japanese with the Kamakura transmission of the Linji lineage as Rinzai Zen, and in Japanese monastic vocabulary 喝! (katsu!) has become iconic — one of the small cluster of terms (along with 参禅 and 公案) by which Zen marks itself in the public mind.

gloss: the Chan staff — the master's teaching stick, wielded as a direct pedagogical instrument that operates at a level prior to discursive speech, emblematically associated with Deshan Xuanjian
notes: 棒 (bō, Ch. bàng) names the wooden staff carried by a Chan master and used as a teaching instrument. In ordinary Chinese the character is simply 'stick, rod, staff'; its Chan-technical specialization turns it into the name of a pedagogical device that operates at a level prior to verbal exchange. The figure associated with 棒 above all others is Deshan Xuanjian (徳山宣鑑, 782–865), a ninth-century Chan master whose teaching method was famously structured around the staff. His defining declaration — 道得也三十棒、道不得也三十棒 ('whether you can say it or not, thirty blows') — compresses the doctrinal point that the staff works at a level orthogonal to whether the student speaks correctly: the axis of right-speech and wrong-speech is simply not the relevant axis, and the staff falls on the student at a location beneath that axis. Deshan's method pairs with Linji Yixuan's shout (喝) as the two great emblematic non-verbal devices of the Tang-dynasty Chan masters, and the pairing is formalized in the later tradition as 棒喝 (bāng hè / bōkatsu), the staff-and-shout complex that names the direct, non-discursive pedagogy of the Linji/Rinzai lineage. The doctrinal claim embedded in the use of the staff is that the content of the teaching cannot be transmitted through discursive speech because the medium of discursive speech is itself what the teaching dismantles. The staff is the instrument by which the teacher demonstrates this claim at the level of pedagogical practice: not by saying it (which would contradict the claim) but by enacting it. The term enters Japanese with the Kamakura transmission of the Linji lineage as Rinzai Zen, and in Japanese monastic vocabulary 棒 carries the full weight of the Deshan tradition — it is not merely a stick but a particular implement whose pedagogical use has a precise history and a specific doctrinal register.

gloss: fly-whisk — a short staff topped with a bundle of animal hair or plant fibers, originally a functional implement for shooing flies and extended in Chan into a ceremonial instrument signifying the master's authority to teach and transmit the dharma
notes: 拂子 (hossu, Ch. fúzǐ) names the fly-whisk — a short staff with a tuft of animal hair (traditionally horse-tail, yak-tail, or white hair) or plant fiber (palm, hemp) bound at its end — used ceremonially in Chan and Zen monastic practice as a signifier of a master's authority. The object has Indian Buddhist origins as a functional monastic implement (the bālavyajana) permitted in the Vinaya as a protection against biting insects and continued by monastics of the early sangha. Its transformation into a ceremonial instrument signifying authority to teach is a specifically Chinese and East Asian development: in the Chan tradition the 拂子 is passed by a master to a designated dharma-heir as one of the signs of transmission, and its being held or raised during a dharma talk (teishō, jōdō) marks the master's speaking position as authoritative. The compound's two characters identify the object functionally: 拂 (to brush away, to sweep, to flick aside) names the action, and 子 (as a nominalizing suffix) turns the action into the instrument that performs it — 'the thing that brushes.' The 拂子 appears frequently in recorded koan dialogues as a handled object that masters raise, hold, set down, or hand to disciples, and these gestures are read as teachings in the literature: the fly-whisk's being held up and the master's silence may together constitute a single pedagogical event. In the later tradition the 拂子 is one of the classical regalia that a Zen master is entitled to carry (alongside the staff 杖, the seal 印, and related items), and its transmission from master to disciple is a physical act in the ceremony of dharma-inheritance (嗣法). The term is part of a broader Chan technical vocabulary for implements that function simultaneously as practical monastic equipment and as ceremonial signifiers of authority, and the dual register — functional object that is also symbolic object — is itself doctrinally important: the tradition insists that the symbolic authority is not superimposed on the practical object but arises from its honest use.

gloss: the ball of doubt — the consolidated, undifferentiated mass of existential questioning that concentrates under sustained koan practice and whose breakthrough is identified with awakening
notes: 疑団 (gidan, Ch. yítuán) names the phase of Chan meditative practice in which the student's discursive doubts — plural, scattered, intellectually formulable — concentrate under the pressure of sustained koan work into a single undifferentiated mass of questioning (the 団, the bounded enclosure) that can no longer be addressed piecewise. The classical source for the concept is Dahui Zonggao (1089–1163), whose Letters (大慧書) give the canonical instructions for kànhuà chán: the student holds the critical phrase (話頭) of a case — paradigmatically Zhaozhou's 無 — and sustains the questioning posture until the scattered surface doubts consolidate into the 疑団. The doctrinal significance of the consolidation is that the 疑団 is no longer a mental object among others but a single total condition of the practitioner, and its resolution is accordingly not an intellectual answer but a breakthrough that reconfigures the practitioner's relation to experience as a whole. Hakuin Ekaku (1686–1768) systematized Dahui's logic into the formula 大疑—大死—大悟 (great doubt, great death, great awakening): the ball of doubt must grow large enough to precipitate the dissolution of the ego-self (the great death) before the awakening (the great realization) can occur. The concept is specifically Rinzai and specifically koan-centered — it presupposes the kanhua method's structured concentration on a critical phrase — and it distinguishes the Rinzai path from the objectless sitting of silent illumination (黙照), where doubt is not the primary medium of practice. In modern Rinzai vocabulary the 疑団 remains the load-bearing term for the productive existential pressure of sustained koan work, and the phrase 疑団を起こす (raising the ball of doubt) is standard for describing the state the practitioner is instructed to cultivate.

gloss: venerable teacher — a fully authorized Zen master who has completed training and received dharma transmission; the standard Japanese Rinzai title for a teacher qualified to direct students in koan study
notes: 老師 (rōshi, Ch. lǎoshī) — literally 'venerable teacher' — pairs the honorific 老 (venerable, old in years or practice) with 師 (teacher as institutional office). In modern Chinese usage 老師 is the ordinary word for schoolteacher and carries no Buddhist specialization. In Japanese, however, the term has a specifically technical Rinzai register: a 老師 is a Zen master who has completed the full koan curriculum, received inka (印可, the master's seal of approval) from their own 老師, and is thereby qualified to direct students through koan practice in dokusan. The title is not assumed but conferred, and the conferral is a definite event in the student's training history: before inka the monk is sōryo or unsui; after inka they are 老師. The Rinzai register differs importantly from the Sōtō honorific 禅師 (zenji), which is applied in Sōtō primarily to the great ancestors of the lineage (Dōgen Zenji, Keizan Zenji) and is rarely used for living teachers in the way 老師 is used for living Rinzai masters. The term's Japanese specialization reflects the Rinzai lineage's emphasis on a particular institutional authority — the authority to direct koan study — and the compound encodes this authority as grounded in the depth of practice that the honorific 老 acknowledges. In the modern Western transmission of Rinzai Zen, from Shaku Sōen and D. T. Suzuki through the twentieth-century teacher-figures, 老師 has become the standard English-language term for a qualified Zen teacher, and the word has entered English monastic vocabulary largely unchanged.

gloss: Zen master — the formal honorific for a great Zen teacher, conferred especially in Sōtō on the lineage's foundational ancestors; in the Chinese tradition often granted by imperial decree as a title of state-recognized eminence
notes: 禅師 (zenji, Ch. chánshī) 'Chan/Zen master' — the formal honorific for a great teacher in the Chan/Zen lineage. The compound pairs 禅 (Chan/Zen meditation, the school built around it) with 師 (teacher as institutional office). The term's register differs importantly from 老師 (rōshi): 禅師 is a formal title, often conferred posthumously or at a particular point in a teacher's career, and in the Chinese tradition it was frequently awarded by imperial decree as a mark of state-recognized eminence. The Song-dynasty Chan masters regularly received imperial 禅師 titles — Dahui Zonggao was granted the title 大慧禅師 (Dàhuì Chánshī) by Emperor Gaozong — and these titles became the standard way of referring to the ancestors in the lamp histories and recorded-sayings collections. In Japanese usage the term is especially associated with Sōtō Zen: Dōgen Zenji (道元禅師, 1200–1253) and Keizan Zenji (瑩山禅師, 1268–1325) are the two foundational honorifics that organize Sōtō's sense of its own lineage, and the repeated use of 禅師 in the Eihei Shingi and other Sōtō monastic texts names the figures whose authority grounds the school's claim to dharma transmission from China. The term's register is more formal and more reverential than 老師: where 老師 names a living institutional office (the teacher currently directing one's training), 禅師 is more likely to name the great ancestor whose teaching the current community inherits, and it can be used for living teachers only in the most formal contexts. Both terms assume 師 as the underlying institutional office; they differ in which register of honor — venerability-in-practice versus formal-eminence-in-the-lineage — they attach to that office.

gloss: preceptor — the monastic teacher responsible for an ordained student's training, especially in matters of Vinaya (monastic discipline); the Sanskrit source of the East Asian title 和尚
notes: उपाध्याय (upādhyāya) is the Sanskrit term in the Vinaya for the monastic preceptor — the teacher who takes responsibility for a novice's ordination, training in monastic rules, and instruction in the fundamentals of the Dharma. In the Indian sangha the upādhyāya is distinguished from the ācārya (teacher in specific subjects, e.g., sutra recitation) and from the kalyāṇamitra (spiritual friend): the upādhyāya is specifically the Vinaya-trained preceptor whose recognition is required for a novice's ordination and whose institutional role is to make the novice a full member of the monastic community. The term entered Chinese via Central Asian intermediaries — the pronunciation 和尚 (héshang in modern Mandarin) preserves a Khotanese or Tocharian rendering of the Sanskrit rather than a direct Sanskrit transliteration, and the characters 和 and 尚 serve phonetically rather than semantically. The compound is thus a record of the specific Central Asian route by which Indian Buddhist monastic vocabulary reached Chinese: the term traveled with the monks and translators of the Silk Road, and its surviving Chinese pronunciation fossilizes that route. In Chinese Buddhist usage 和尚 was generalized to the ordinary term for a fully ordained Buddhist priest — the monk whose training is complete enough to have preceptorial responsibility for others — and this generalization obscured the original Vinaya specificity. The term enters Japanese in all major Buddhist schools but diverges in pronunciation: Zen and most schools read 和尚 as おしょう (oshō), Tendai reads it as かしょう (kashō), and Shingon reads it as わじょう (wajō). The divergence reflects the separate transmission histories of these schools and the different Chinese source texts they read: all three pronunciations are attempts to give Japanese readings to a compound that was already, in Chinese, a transliteration rather than a native word.

gloss: head cook of a Chan/Zen monastery — one of the six principal monastic officers (六知事 roku chiji) responsible for the preparation of the community's meals; in Sōtō tradition the office is doctrinally elevated through Dōgen's Tenzo Kyōkun as itself the expression of awakened practice
notes: 典座 (Ch. diǎnzuò, Jp. tenzo) names the office of the head cook in the Chinese Chan monastic system. The compound is an indigenous Chinese institutional creation with no Sanskrit antecedent: it develops within the monastic regulations of the Tang and Song dynasties as Chan communities organize themselves around the meditation hall and the kitchen as the two centers of monastic life. The compound pairs 典 (the entrusted office, the standing responsibility) with 座 (the seat that names the institutional position): the tenzo is the monk formally entrusted with the standing seat of the kitchen, distinguished from rotational kitchen helpers by the durability of the office. The institutional importance of the office reflects the practical centrality of food preparation to a large training community — the tenzo feeds dozens or hundreds of monks several times a day, and the rhythm of the kitchen shapes the rhythm of the entire monastery. In the Chinese Chan system the tenzo is one of the six principal officers (六知事): 都寺 (general administrator), 監寺 (deputy administrator), 副寺 (treasurer), 維那 (officer of the meditation hall), 典座 (head cook), and 直歳 (chief steward). Dōgen's importation of the Chinese system into Japanese Sōtō practice preserves this six-officer structure and elevates the tenzo specifically through his Tenzo Kyōkun (典座教訓, 'Instructions to the Cook,' 1237), which articulates the office as the very expression of practice-realization. The Tenzo Kyōkun's claim that the cook's careful attention to a single grain of rice is itself the working of awakened mind establishes the doctrinal frame within which the tenzo's office becomes one of the most theologically charged in the Sōtō system — not a lesser practical role but a paradigm for the integration of work and practice.

gloss: monastic officer responsible for the assignment of communal duties; in Chinese Chan transformed into the supervisor of the meditation hall, chanting services, and the overall rhythm of monastic life
notes: कर्मदान (karmadāna, 'duty-giver') is the Sanskrit Vinaya term for the monastic officer who assigns daily and rotational duties within the saṅgha — the figure responsible for distributing the practical work of the community and ensuring that obligations are met. The term combines karma (action, work, duty) with dāna (giving, assignment), and names the institutional role of organizing how labor and ritual responsibility are shared among the monks of a community. In the Indian Vinaya the karmadāna is one of the standard administrative officers of a settled monastic community, and the role is preserved in the Chinese reception of the Vinaya as 維那 (Ch. wéinà). The compound 維那 is a half-transliteration: 維 carries semantic weight (the binding cord that holds the community together, doing double duty by transliterating the Sanskrit karma-syllable while also meaningfully naming the binding work) while 那 is purely phonetic (rendering the dā syllable). In Chinese Chan monastic practice the office's responsibilities expanded substantially beyond the original Vinaya assignment-of-duties: the wéinà becomes the supervisor of the meditation hall, the leader of the chanting services, and the officer responsible for the overall rhythm of the monastic schedule — a development reflecting the Chan tradition's reorganization of monastic life around the meditation hall as the practical center of practice. The Japanese reading いの (ino) preserves a Tang-era pronunciation of the compound (parallel to how 和尚 preserves a Khotanese-mediated pronunciation of upādhyāya), and the 維那 is one of the six principal officers (六知事) of a Zen training monastery in both Sōtō and Rinzai traditions, with responsibilities specific to the conduct of zazen, the timing of services, and the leading of communal chanting.

gloss: head seat — the senior student appointed for an ango (practice period), who shares teaching responsibility with the abbot and undergoes the dharma combat ceremony (hossenshiki) at its conclusion
notes: 首座 (Ch. shǒuzuò, Jp. shuso) names the office of the senior practitioner appointed to occupy the position of honor at the head of the meditation hall during a practice period (安居 ango). The compound pairs 首 (the head, the leading position) with 座 (the institutional seat) — together the figure of the head seat in the assembly's two parallel rows of meditators, the position from which the senior student is visibly recognized as the practice-period's leading figure.
