The office develops within the Chinese Chan monastic regulations as a structural transition stage in monastic training: the shuso is no longer a student under the teacher's instruction in the ordinary sense but is also not yet a teacher in their own right; rather, they share for the duration of the practice period a portion of the teacher's instructional authority — leading sections of the schedule, giving informal instruction to junior monks, and serving as a model for the assembly. The office is codified for Japanese Sōtō practice by Dōgen's Eihei Shingi, whose Chiji Shingi articulates the shuso as one of the principal officers of the practice period and whose conclusion is marked by the 法戦式 (hossenshiki, dharma combat ceremony) in which the shuso publicly responds to questions from the assembly from the high seat. The hossenshiki is structurally the public testimony to what the shuso's office has accomplished: the shuso has undergone the work of the practice period and is now able to function as a respondent rather than a questioner, a transformation the assembly witnesses in the choreographed exchange of formal challenges. In Rinzai practice the office serves a similar institutional function, with comparable ceremonial culmination. The shuso office is therefore not a permanent rank but a temporary appointment whose meaning is local to a single practice period — a particular monk holds the office for the duration of one ango and then returns to ordinary monastic standing — and this temporal bounding is part of what makes the office work as a transition stage in the longer training trajectory.

gloss: monastic officer responsible for discipline and timekeeping in the meditation hall; in Rinzai monasteries second only to the rōshi in authority within the zendō, wielding the keisaku and maintaining the hall's atmosphere of disciplined silence
notes: 直日 (Ch. zhírì, Jp. jikijitsu) names the office of the monk on duty for the day in the Chinese Chan monastic system — a position whose responsibilities concentrate on the immediate, on-the-spot functioning of the meditation hall. The compound pairs 直 (on-the-spot, immediately responsible) with 日 (the day) and originally named a rotational office whose holder cycled through days of duty in the assigned order. In Japanese Rinzai monastic practice the responsibility evolves from a rotational position into a more durable institutional role: the jikijitsu is the disciplinarian of the meditation hall, responsible for the timing of zazen periods, the conduct of the monks during sitting, the wielding of the 警策 (keisaku, the encouragement stick used to strike drowsy or improperly-postured meditators), and the overall maintenance of the hall's atmosphere of disciplined silence. In contemporary Rinzai monasteries the jikijitsu is second only to the rōshi in authority within the zendō and exercises a substantial portion of the practical disciplinary direction of the assembly. The compound preserves the rotational logic of its origin even as the institutional reality has stabilized into a longer-term assignment: the figure of the monk-of-the-day, whose attention is fixed on the immediate practical functioning of the hall, names the office's specifically tactical scope. The office's prominence in Rinzai reflects the Rinzai tradition's emphasis on disciplinary intensity and on the structured choreography of the zendō as a training environment; in Sōtō practice the equivalent functions are distributed among other officers — the 維那 (ino) handles much of the timing and chanting, and the 直歳 (shissui, the chief steward) covers the longer-term oversight — and the jikijitsu as a single concentrated office is more characteristic of the Rinzai monastic system.

gloss: the personal attendant of an abbot or senior teacher in a Chan/Zen monastery; the monk who stands closest to the master, mediating access, carrying the master's words, and serving the master's daily needs as part of a training relationship
notes: 侍者 (Ch. shìzhě, Jp. jisha) names the monastic office of personal attendant to a senior teacher — typically the abbot of a training monastery, or sometimes a particularly venerated rōshi within a non-abbatial role. The compound pairs 侍 (to attend, to wait upon) with 者 (the one who) and is therefore literally 'the one who attends.' The office originates in the Chinese imperial bureaucracy, where 侍者 named the junior official in personal attendance on a higher minister, and is reapplied in Chan monastic vocabulary to the parallel function within the monastery: the monk in close personal service to the master. The institutional structure of the office is precisely calibrated. The jisha is responsible for the abbot's daily practical needs (preparing tea, arranging the abbot's quarters, attending meals), for managing the abbot's schedule (announcing visitors, directing students to dokusan, coordinating ceremonial duties), and for serving as the practical interface between the abbot and the rest of the monastery (carrying messages to officers, communicating the abbot's directives to the assembly). In Rinzai practice the jisha specifically directs students to dokusan: the practitioner who wishes to enter the interview room first encounters the jisha, who manages the queue and confirms the appropriate moment of entry. The office is doctrinally significant beyond its practical functions because of the training relationship it constitutes. The jisha lives in continuous proximity to the master, observes the master's conduct in unguarded moments, and absorbs through this sustained close exposure something of the master's mode of practice that cannot be transmitted in the formal teaching encounters alone. The jisha office is therefore typically a stage in the longer training trajectory of a senior monk, not a permanent role: a monk holds the jisha office for a defined period as part of preparation for eventual leadership, and the office's combination of practical service and training intimacy is structurally important to the way Chan/Zen lineages reproduce themselves. The compound preserves the institutional logic across both Sōtō and Rinzai practice, and the office name remains identical in Korean Sŏn (시자) and Vietnamese Thiền.

gloss: a Zen monk in training; literally 'clouds and water,' evoking the wandering monk who drifts like clouds and flows like water through the geography of monasteries, masters, and practice situations
notes: 雲水 (Ch. yúnshuǐ, Jp. unsui) is one of the most poetically saturated terms in the Chan/Zen monastic vocabulary. The compound pairs 雲 (clouds) with 水 (water) and is etymologically and grammatically a copulative compound: not 'cloudy water' or 'water in the clouds' but 'clouds and water' as a paired figure. The figure draws on a deep classical Chinese poetic register in which the wandering recluse is identified with these two natural elements: clouds drift across the sky without attachment to location, water flows across the terrain without attachment to form, and the figure who lives in this drifting-and-flowing manner is the one whose practice is not bound to a single fixed setting. Chan inherits this register from the broader Chinese poetic tradition (Du Fu, the Tang recluse poets, the Daoist literature on the wandering sage) and gives it specifically monastic application. The 雲水 is the monk in training who travels — specifically, the monk who has left the immediate teacher and is undertaking the period of pilgrimage among masters and monasteries that the Chan tradition treats as essential to genuine training. Historically this period was extensive: a Tang or Song monk might spend many years walking among the major Chan monasteries of southern China, presenting himself to a series of masters, attempting to deepen his practice through encounter with different teachers and lineages, and eventually settling under the master with whom genuine transmission was possible. The Japanese Rinzai and Sōtō traditions inherit this institutional pattern in modified form: the contemporary unsui is a monk in formation in a training monastery, and while the literal pilgrimage component has diminished, the term preserves its etymological force as a description of the unfixed mode of life proper to the training period. The unsui's traditional traveling robes, the wide straw hat, and the small bundle of belongings are the practical expressions of the cloud-and-water figure — the monk's possessions are limited to what can be carried, and the location is not fixed. The term operates in two registers simultaneously: institutionally, it names a definite stage in the monastic training trajectory (the period of formal training before full ordination and the assumption of permanent monastic responsibilities), and poetically, it names a mode of life characterized by drifting unattachment. The two registers reinforce each other: the institutional period is structurally calibrated to be the period during which the poetic mode of life is appropriate.

gloss: the meditation hall of a Chan/Zen monastery — the institutional space in which zazen is practiced, distinct from the dharma hall (法堂) where formal teaching is delivered and from the monks' hall (僧堂) where the residential aspects of monastic life are conducted
notes: 禅堂 (Ch. chántáng, Jp. zendō) names the meditation hall as a distinct institutional space within the architectural and ritual organization of a Chan/Zen monastery. The compound pairs 禅 (Chan/meditation) with 堂 (hall) and is grammatically straightforward: the hall in which 禅 (meditation) is conducted. The institutional location of the zendō is precisely calibrated. In the traditional Chan monastic plan the central axis of the monastery typically runs from the entrance gate (山門) through the Buddha hall (仏殿) and the dharma hall (法堂), with the residential and practice halls organized to either side. The zendō is one of the principal practice halls, and its architectural features are functional: long platforms (単 tan) on either side of a central aisle on which the practitioners sit in zazen, sleep, and take meals, with each practitioner's tan position assigned for the duration of the practice period. The hall's choreography is highly structured — the entrance, the placement of cushions, the timing of bells, the movement between sitting and walking meditation — and the zendō as a space is the institutional embodiment of this choreography. In contemporary Japanese practice there is a distinction between 禅堂 (zendō) and 僧堂 (sōdō) that is sometimes blurred but is institutionally significant. In strict Sōtō usage the 僧堂 is the combined hall in which the monks meditate, sleep, and eat (the full residential meditation hall), while 禅堂 sometimes names a hall used primarily for meditation without the residential function — particularly in lay practice centers, smaller temples, or training facilities outside the main training monasteries. The two terms are used interchangeably in many contexts, and the distinction is often more historical or stylistic than functionally rigorous, but the underlying difference matters for understanding the architectural typology: a 僧堂 is a fully residential meditation hall belonging to a training monastery, while a 禅堂 may or may not include the residential functions depending on the institution. The compound 禅堂 has been adopted into English as a standard loanword (zendō), where it usually names the meditation hall of any Zen practice institution regardless of whether the residential function is present.

gloss: the combined residential meditation hall of a traditional Chan/Zen training monastery — the space in which the monks meditate, sleep, and eat, organizing the entire residential practice of the assembly around the rhythm of zazen
notes: 僧堂 (Ch. sēngtáng, Jp. sōdō) names the combined residential meditation hall that is the institutional center of a traditional Chan/Zen training monastery. The compound pairs 僧 (monks) with 堂 (hall) and is doctrinally precise: the hall belongs to the monks as the assembly of individual practitioners (rather than to the abstract saṅgha as such), and within it the entirety of the monk's residential and meditative life is conducted. The architectural and ritual specifics of the sōdō are highly elaborated. Long raised platforms (単 tan) line the walls of the hall, and each monk is assigned a fixed tan position for the duration of the practice period. On this single space of approximately one tatami mat the monk sits in zazen, sleeps at night, takes formal meals (oryōki) during the day, and performs the small daily rituals that punctuate the schedule. The integration of meditation, sleep, and meals into a single space is doctrinally important: the sōdō embodies the principle that practice is not confined to formal sitting periods but extends across the whole rhythm of daily life, and the architectural form of the hall is what makes this integration concrete. The sōdō is presided over by the 維那 (ino), who manages the timing of the hall's activities through the bells and wooden blocks that signal the transitions between zazen, meals, sleep, and ritual chanting. The institutional centrality of the sōdō to traditional training monasteries cannot be overstated: in a fully traditional Sōtō or Rinzai training monastery the sōdō is where the training actually happens, and a monk's training is structured by the years spent in the hall under the discipline of its schedule. The compound is sometimes used loosely to refer to a Zen training monastery as a whole (the 専門僧堂 senmon sōdō, 'specialized training monastery,' is the official designation for institutions authorized to ordain and train monks), reflecting the way the hall stands metonymically for the whole training institution. The institutional distinction between 僧堂 and 禅堂 (zendō, meditation hall) is significant: the 僧堂 specifically combines the residential and meditative functions in the traditional training-monastery format, while a 禅堂 may be a meditation-only hall in a non-residential setting.

gloss: the dharma hall of a Chan/Zen monastery — the institutional space in which the abbot delivers formal lectures (jōdō, teishō) to the assembled community, distinct from the meditation hall (zendō) and the monks' hall (sōdō)
notes: 法堂 (Ch. fǎtáng, Jp. hattō) names the dharma hall of a Chan/Zen monastery as the architectural and institutional space in which formal teaching is delivered. The compound pairs 法 (dharma) with 堂 (hall) and is institutionally precise: the hall is dedicated specifically to the formal articulation of dharma, distinct from the meditation hall (禅堂) where zazen is practiced and from the monks' hall (僧堂) where the residential aspects of monastic life are conducted. In the traditional Chan monastic plan the central axis of the monastery typically runs from the entrance gate (山門) through the Buddha hall (仏殿) to the dharma hall (法堂), with the dharma hall occupying the architectural and ritual culmination of the central axis. The hall is dominated by the high seat (高座, kōza), an elevated throne from which the abbot delivers formal discourses, and the institutional choreography of the hall is calibrated to the abbot's ascent of this seat (上堂, jōdō, ascending the hall). The dharma hall is the architectural setting for the most formal teaching events of the monastic calendar: the morning convocations on the first and fifteenth of each month, the seasonal opening and closing of practice periods, the ceremonies attending dharma transmission, and the formal funerary rites for the abbot. Dōgen's Eihei Kōroku preserves an extensive record of the discourses he delivered in the dharma hall at Kōshōji and Eiheiji, and the textual genre of the recorded saying (語録, goroku) takes its institutional shape from the architectural and ritual form of the dharma hall: the goroku is the textual transcription of discourses delivered from the high seat, and the genre's literary conventions (the formal opening, the climactic verse, the closing gesture with the staff or whisk) reflect the choreography of the dharma hall as a ritual space. The institutional distinction between the dharma hall and the meditation hall is doctrinally important: it preserves the difference between the formal articulation of dharma (which the dharma hall houses) and the meditative practice of dharma (which the meditation hall houses), and the architectural separation makes this distinction concrete. In Korean Sŏn the corresponding hall is the 법당 (Pŏptang) and in Vietnamese Thiền the Pháp đường, with the same institutional function preserved across the East Asian Chan transmission.

gloss: the triple gate at the formal entrance to a Chan/Zen monastery — the architectural threshold whose three openings symbolize the three gates of liberation (emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness), and the institutional boundary marking entry into the monastic precincts
notes: 三門 (Ch. sānmén, Jp. sanmon), also written 山門 (mountain gate), is the formal entrance gate of a Chan/Zen monastery — a multi-leveled gate-structure with three openings that constitutes both the architectural threshold of the monastic precincts and a doctrinal symbol carried in monumental form. The two written forms 三門 and 山門 are read identically and refer to the same architectural structure, but the alternation preserves a doctrinal ambiguity: 三門 emphasizes the gate's three openings as a symbol of the three gates of liberation (三解脱門, sangedatsumon: 空 emptiness, 無相 signlessness, 無願 wishlessness) drawn from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā literature, while 山門 emphasizes the gate's location at the foot of the mountain on which the monastery is built and identifies the gate metonymically with the monastery itself. In practice both registers are operative simultaneously, and the doctrinal symbolism of the triple opening is preserved even when the gate is referred to as the mountain gate. The architectural form of the sanmon is highly elaborate. The gate is typically a two-story structure with three openings at ground level — a central opening flanked by two lateral openings — and an upper level containing a Buddha hall in which images of Śākyamuni, the sixteen arhats, and various protective deities are enshrined. The gate is one of the largest and most monumental structures in a major Zen monastery: the sanmon at Tōfukuji and Nanzenji in Kyoto, both designated National Treasures, are among the largest wooden gate-structures in Japan and rise to over twenty meters in height. The institutional significance of the gate is that crossing its threshold constitutes the formal entry into the monastic precincts, and the gate is therefore the architectural embodiment of the boundary between the lay world and the monastic life. Ceremonies of monastic entry, of welcoming visiting teachers, and of receiving major gifts to the monastery are conducted at the sanmon, and the gate's monumental form is institutionally calibrated to these functions. In contemporary Sōtō and Rinzai monasteries the sanmon remains the formal entrance and is opened on ceremonial occasions while the lateral pedestrian gates are used for daily passage. The doctrinal symbolism of the three openings as the three gates of liberation has been articulated continuously in Chan/Zen commentary: passing through the central opening is figured as the practitioner's passage through emptiness (空) into the monastic life of practice, and the lateral openings extend the symbolism through the remaining gates of liberation (signlessness 無相 and wishlessness 無願).

gloss: a Chan/Zen master's formal certification that a student has completed training and attained authentic realization — the seal of approval impressed upon the student's awakening as a documentary authentication of its genuineness
notes: 印可 (Ch. yìnkě, Jp. inka), often rendered in full as 印可証明 (inka shōmei, 'seal of approval certifying realization'), is the formal Chan/Zen institutional act by which a master certifies that a disciple has completed training and attained authentic realization. The compound pairs 印 (seal, the figure of authoritative authentication) with 可 (formal sanction, what is permitted or affirmed) and is grammatically a verb-object construction: the master impresses the seal of formal sanction upon the disciple's realization, authenticating it as genuine. The figure draws on the legal and bureaucratic vocabulary of imperial Chinese administration, where official documents carried authority through the impression of seals; Chan applies this institutional logic to dharma-recognition and produces a vocabulary in which awakening is figured as a document and the master's recognition as the authenticating seal. The institutional function of inka is doctrinally precise. The student who has worked through the koan curriculum, demonstrated realization across the full range of cases, and continued practice to a level the master judges adequate is granted inka as the formal mark of completed training. Inka is therefore not the recognition of a single moment of awakening but the recognition of a sustained transformation that has matured to the point where the student is qualified to teach in the master's name. The Rinzai lineage in particular has elaborated inka into a formal institutional act: the inka is conferred in a ceremony, accompanied by the presentation of formal documents (the 印可状, inka-jō, certificate of inka), and constitutes the student's promotion to full standing within the lineage. In the Sōtō lineage the parallel institutional act is more often referred to as 嗣法 (shihō, dharma succession) and is connected to the formal documents of dharma transmission (嗣書, shisho), with the term inka used less frequently. The conceptual content of inka has been the subject of considerable reflection within the Chan/Zen tradition itself. The institutional act of inka can in principle become routinized — granted as a matter of seniority rather than as a recognition of authentic realization — and the tradition has been alert to this possibility from the Tang dynasty onward. The literature of Chan recorded sayings includes recurrent warnings against the granting of inka where the realization is not genuine, and the relationship between the institutional structure of inka and the actual transformation it is meant to certify has been a recurrent theme of Chan self-criticism. The contemporary reception of Zen in the West has continued this self-critical tradition, with extensive discussion of cases in which institutional inka has been granted in the absence of the realization the institutional form is meant to mark. The compound preserves its institutional precision across Sōtō, Rinzai, Korean Sŏn (인가), and Vietnamese Thiền (ấn khả), with the figure of the seal-impressed authentication remaining stable across the East Asian Chan transmission.

gloss: the formal acknowledgment of a disciple as a dharma-heir of the master — the institutional act of dharma-succession that constitutes the disciple as the legitimate continuator of the master's lineage and the practical mechanism by which the Chan/Zen lineage reproduces itself across generations
notes: 嗣法 (Ch. sìfǎ, Jp. shihō) is the formal Chan/Zen institutional act by which a master acknowledges a disciple as the legitimate dharma-heir of the master's lineage. The compound pairs 嗣 (to succeed, to inherit, the verb of legitimate generational continuation) with 法 (dharma) and is doctrinally precise: the disciple is constituted as the dharma-heir of the master in a structural relationship modeled on the patrilineal succession of the Chinese family. The compound is grammatically a verb-object construction in which 嗣 (to inherit) acts upon 法 (dharma): the disciple inherits the dharma from the master, and the institutional act of shihō is what constitutes this inheritance. Shihō is the central mechanism by which the Chan/Zen lineage reproduces itself across generations, and the institutional structure depends on the analogy with familial succession: just as the eldest son in the Chinese family inherits position, title, and ritual obligation from the father, so the dharma-heir in the Chan lineage inherits the dharma-position, the lineage-title, and the ritual obligations of teaching and transmission from the master. The institutional documentation of shihō is highly elaborated. Each dharma-heir receives a 血脈 (kechimyaku, the blood-vein chart) tracing the lineage from Śākyamuni through the Indian and Chinese patriarchs to the present master and now to the heir, and a 嗣書 (shisho, the document of succession) formally certifying the heir's status as the master's legitimate continuator. These documents are themselves doctrinally weighted: Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō fascicle 嗣書 (Shisho) is a sustained meditation on the document of succession as the institutional embodiment of the dharma-transmission, and the document is treated as a sacred object whose transmission is a doctrinally significant act. The institutional distinction between shihō and inka (印可) is somewhat fluid across lineages and traditions but is not without significance. In Sōtō Zen the term shihō is the standard term for the formal succession act, and it is closely tied to the documents of dharma-transmission and the practice period (ango) following which dharma-succession is conferred. In Rinzai Zen the term inka tends to be used more frequently for the master's certification of completed koan training, with shihō reserved for the more formal institutional act of designating a particular disciple as the lineage-successor. The two terms are conceptually distinct: inka is the certification of realization, while shihō is the constitution of the disciple as the lineage-heir, and a disciple may receive inka without being designated as the formal shihō-heir who will inherit the master's temple and lineage-position. The doctrinal weight of shihō is considerable. The Chan/Zen claim that the dharma is transmitted from master to disciple — and that the lineage is therefore the structural chain of these transmissions — depends on the institutional rigor of shihō. If the institutional act is corrupted or routinized, the lineage's claim to authentic transmission is correspondingly weakened, and the tradition has been alert to this possibility from the Tang dynasty onward. The contemporary Sōtō Zen system continues to enact shihō as the formal mechanism by which dharma-succession is conferred, and the institution remains the central means by which the Sōtō lineage reproduces itself.

gloss: impermanence — the absence of permanence in any conditioned phenomenon; the foundational mark of saṃsāric existence and the first of the Three Dharma Seals (along with anātman and duḥkha), establishing the basic Buddhist claim that no compounded thing endures
notes: Sanskrit anitya, the privative form of nitya (permanent, eternal), is the technical Buddhist term for the universal impermanence of all conditioned phenomena. The doctrinal claim is precise: no compounded thing — no aggregate of conditions, no being, no mental state, no phenomenon arising in dependence on causes — endures unchanged through time. The teaching of anitya is foundational across all schools of Buddhism and is the first of the Three Dharma Seals (Sanskrit trilakṣaṇa, Chinese 三法印, Japanese sanbōin), the criteria by which a teaching is identified as Buddhist. The Chinese 無常 (Ch. wúcháng, Jp. mujō) is a calque that pairs 無 (no, without) with 常 (constant, eternal), preserving the privative grammatical structure of the Sanskrit. The compound is doctrinally precise but generates an interesting tension within East Asian Buddhism: 常 (the unchanging, the eternal) is also a positive attribute of certain Mahāyāna concepts — Buddha-nature, the Tathāgatagarbha, nirvāṇa — which Tathāgatagarbha-influenced sutras affirm as 常住 (eternally abiding). The relationship between the universal 無常 of conditioned phenomena and the asserted 常 of unconditioned realities has generated centuries of doctrinal exegesis, with positions ranging from the strict Madhyamaka denial that anything is 常 in any sense to the Tathāgatagarbha affirmation of a 常 that is not the negation of 無常 but its true mode. Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō fascicle 'Busshō' takes a distinctive position in this debate, identifying impermanence with Buddha-nature itself in the formula 無常仏性 (mujō busshō): the conditioned arising and passing of phenomena is not the obstacle to Buddha-nature but is Buddha-nature in its actual mode. The Japanese literary register of mujō is particularly rich, supplying the affective vocabulary of Heian and Kamakura Buddhist literature: the Hōjōki opens with the celebrated image of the river that flows ceaselessly without its waters being the same waters; the Heike Monogatari opens with 諸行無常 (shogyō mujō, all conditioned things are impermanent); the Kamakura sense of mujō shapes the aesthetic of medieval Japanese literature in a way that exceeds the strictly doctrinal use of the term.

gloss: birth-and-death — the cycle of conditioned existence figured as the alternation of birth (jāti) and death (maraṇa); a synonym for saṃsāra emphasizing the temporal-experiential structure of cyclic existence as the recurring movement from arising to passing rather than the spatial figure of the wheel
notes: Sanskrit jāti-maraṇa is the technical Buddhist term-pair for the cycle of conditioned existence understood as the recurring alternation of birth and death across lifetimes. In the doctrinal architecture of the twelve-link chain of dependent origination (十二因縁, dvādaśa-aṅga-pratītyasamutpāda), jāti (birth) is the eleventh link and jarā-maraṇa (old age and death) is the twelfth, and the pair functions as the experiential terminus of the chain — the suffering that conditioned arising produces and that the entire chain leads up to. The Chinese 生死 (Ch. shēngsǐ, Jp. shōji) is the standard calque, pairing 生 (birth, arising) with 死 (death, ceasing) in a verb-pair that names the cycle by its two poles. The compound is functionally synonymous with 輪廻 (rinne, the wheel of transmigration) but emphasizes a different aspect of the same condition: where 輪廻 figures saṃsāra as a wheel turning through realms, 生死 figures it as the temporal alternation of arising and ceasing, the rhythm by which conditioned phenomena come-to-be and pass-away. In ordinary Buddhist doctrinal usage the two compounds are largely interchangeable, with 生死 carrying more of the existential-experiential register and 輪廻 carrying more of the cosmological-mechanical register. Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō fascicle 'Shōji' takes a distinctive position on the compound that marks it as one of the most doctrinally important in his vocabulary. The fascicle refuses both the ordinary view that birth and death are real transitions to be feared and the abstract view that they are illusion to be transcended; Dōgen's claim is that birth and death must be lived as the very activity of Buddha-nature, not as conditions to escape from but as the actual mode of buddha-being. The fascicle's celebrated formula — 'just understand that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa' — collapses the standard Buddhist opposition between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa and articulates the Sōtō claim that liberation is found within the cycle of birth and death, not apart from it. The Japanese reading of the compound is doubled: shōji is the standard Buddhist reading, while seishi can also be used in non-Buddhist contexts for life-and-death in the secular sense; the Buddhist register is reserved for shōji.

gloss: the wheel of transmigration — the cycle of rebirth through the six realms (deva, asura, human, animal, hungry ghost, hell) figured as a turning wheel; the cosmological-mechanical figure of conditioned existence from which awakening liberates beings
notes: Sanskrit saṃsāra, from the verbal root sṛ- (to flow) with the prefix sam- (together, continuously), names the continuous flowing-on of conditioned existence through repeated births. The doctrinal content is precise: beings, propelled by karma and ignorance (avidyā), wander through the six realms of existence — the gods (deva), demigods (asura), humans (manuṣya), animals (tiryak), hungry ghosts (preta), and hell-beings (naraka) — taking new births in accordance with the karmic conditions accumulated in previous lives. The wandering is beginningless and continues until the practitioner attains awakening, which severs the conditions of further rebirth and releases the practitioner from the cycle. The Chinese 輪廻 (Ch. lúnhuí, Jp. rinne) calques the spatial figure of the wheel: 輪 (wheel) pairs with 廻 (to revolve, to turn) to produce a compound naming the wheel's continuous turning, the cyclic motion that carries beings from one birth to the next. The figure is reinforced iconographically by the wheel-of-life images (六道輪廻図, rokudō rinne-zu) that depict the six realms as the segments of a wheel held in the jaws of impermanence — a visual elaboration of the doctrine that became standard in East Asian and Tibetan Buddhist art. The compound is functionally synonymous with 生死 (shōji, birth-and-death) but carries a different conceptual emphasis: where shōji figures saṃsāra as the temporal alternation of arising and ceasing, rinne figures it as a spatial-cosmological wheel turning through the realms. In Pure Land and Tendai contexts the compound 輪廻 carries the strongest doctrinal weight as the condition from which Amida's vow or the dharma's teaching liberates beings, while in Zen contexts the term is used somewhat less frequently than shōji, since the Zen tradition tends to emphasize the immediate experiential register of birth-and-death over the cosmological architecture of the six realms. The compound is current in Chinese (输回, 轮回 in simplified script), Korean (윤회, yunhoe), and Vietnamese (luân hồi) Buddhist vocabulary, with the figure of the wheel preserved across the East Asian transmission. In modern Japanese ordinary usage rinne carries primarily the Buddhist sense and is not used in secular contexts.

gloss: the latter or final dharma age — the third and final stage of the post-Buddha periodization of history, an age of degenerate dharma in which the Buddha's teaching survives in form but no longer produces its full liberating effect; the doctrinal frame within which the Kamakura Buddhist reform movements positioned their teachings
notes: Sanskrit saddharma-vipralopa (the destruction or disappearance of the true dharma) is the technical term for the degenerate condition of the post-Buddha dharma-age in which the Buddha's teaching survives in attenuated and ineffective form. The doctrinal content is precise: in the periodization of post-Buddha history into three eras — 正法 (shōbō, the age of the true dharma), 像法 (zōbō, the age of the semblance dharma), and 末法 (mappō, the age of the final or latter dharma) — mappō is the third and final stage, characterized by the survival of the dharma's outward forms (texts, institutions, ritual practices) without their inward efficacy. The lengths of the three ages vary across sources, but the standard Japanese reckoning, derived from the Mahāmāyā Sūtra and other texts and elaborated by medieval Tendai scholars, places the onset of mappō at 1052 CE — roughly fifteen hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa under the long reckoning standard in East Asia. The doctrine generates significant practical consequences. If the dharma's full efficacy has degenerated, the practices that liberated beings in earlier ages may no longer be adequate to the diminished spiritual capacities of beings in mappō. The Pure Land tradition draws the strongest conclusions: Hōnen's argument in the Senchakushū is that in mappō self-power practice (jiriki) — the cultivation of meditation, ethical discipline, and wisdom — is no longer sufficient to attain liberation, and that only the other-power (tariki) of Amida's vow, accessed through the simple practice of nenbutsu, remains efficacious. Shinran radicalizes this position in the Kyōgyōshinshō, arguing that even nenbutsu must be received as Amida's gift rather than performed as the practitioner's act. Nichiren, by contrast, identifies the practice of mappō with chanting the title of the Lotus Sutra (daimoku) as the one teaching adequate to the degenerate age. The Zen tradition takes a distinctive position: Dōgen's Bendōwa explicitly argues that the dharma is not subject to the ordinary categories of historical decline, and that for one who undertakes serious practice the conditions of mappō are not different from those of the age of the true dharma; the teaching that mappō has rendered authentic practice impossible is a self-fulfilling delusion that the practitioner must refuse. Saichō's Mappō Tōmyōki (末法燈明記, 'Lamp of the Latter Dharma'), an early Japanese articulation of the doctrine attributed to the Tendai founder, became one of the most widely cited treatises on mappō across the Kamakura reform schools and is the textual source for the standard 1052 dating. The doctrine reshapes the entire intellectual environment of medieval Japanese Buddhism, and the Kamakura reformers — Hōnen, Shinran, Dōgen, Nichiren, Eisai — each position their teaching in relation to it, accepting, refusing, or radically reinterpreting the claim that the contemporary age is one of diminished dharma.

term: sarva-saṃskārā anityāḥ / sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā / zhū xíng wúcháng / shogyō mujō
gloss: all conditioned things are impermanent — the canonical formulation of the first of the Three Dharma Seals, asserting universal impermanence of every compounded phenomenon as the criterion by which a teaching is identified as Buddhist; the doctrinal claim in its full quantified form rather than the bare term anitya
notes: Sanskrit sarva-saṃskārā anityāḥ (Pali sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā) is the canonical formulation of the first of the Three Dharma Seals (trilakṣaṇa, Chinese 三法印, Japanese sanbōin) — the criteria, articulated as three propositions, by which a teaching is identified as Buddhist. The doctrinal architecture is precise. The three seals are: (1) sarva-saṃskārā anityāḥ — all conditioned things are impermanent (諸行無常); (2) sarva-dharmā anātmānaḥ — all dharmas are without self (諸法無我); (3) nirvāṇam śāntam — nirvāṇa is quiescent (涅槃寂静). The first seal is the universal-quantified form of the term anitya (impermanence): where anitya is the bare predicate, sarva-saṃskārā anityāḥ is the full doctrinal claim, asserting that the predicate holds across the entire class of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) without exception. The Sanskrit saṃskāra is one of the most polysemous terms in Buddhist vocabulary, but in this canonical formulation it carries the broad sense of 'compounded thing' or 'conditioned phenomenon' — anything that comes into being through the convergence of conditions and therefore lacks the unconditioned status that would make it exempt from impermanence. The Chinese 諸行 (Ch. zhū xíng, Jp. shogyō) is a calque that pairs 諸 (all, the various) with 行 (here in the technical Buddhist sense of saṃskāra rather than the ordinary sense of action or practice), and the full compound 諸行無常 preserves the universal quantification of the Sanskrit. The compound's transmission into Japanese carries an unusual dual register. As doctrinal claim it operates in the technical scholastic vocabulary of all Japanese Buddhist schools, articulating the foundational Buddhist position that no compounded phenomenon endures unchanged. As literary-aesthetic phrase it occupies a position in Japanese cultural memory that no other Buddhist formula matches: the Heike Monogatari opens with the phrase 諸行無常, and the bell of Gion-shōja resounding the impermanence of all conditioned things becomes one of the most celebrated openings in Japanese literature. The phrase's literary fame in Japan exceeds its purely doctrinal weight and gives it a cultural resonance that the simpler term mujō does not match — 諸行無常 is doctrinal claim and literary topos in a single compound, and its Japanese reception cannot be separated from the Heike Monogatari's framing of medieval Japanese history as a meditation on impermanence.

gloss: departing the world — the death poem composed by a Zen master, samurai, or poet at the point of death, expressing a final settlement of accounts with practice, the world, and the moment of dying; a Japanese cultural-literary genre with no direct foreign antecedent, developed within the Zen monastic context and extended across the broader literary culture of the medieval and early modern periods
notes: Not a translation from Sanskrit or any foreign source but a Japanese cultural-literary genre developed within the medieval Zen monastic context and extended across the broader literary culture of the Muromachi, Edo, and early modern periods. The term 辞世 literally means 'taking leave of the world' and names a tightly-conventionalized poetic form: a single compressed utterance — typically a waka (5-7-5-7-7) or kanshi (Chinese-language verse) and in later periods often a haiku (5-7-5) — composed by the dying person at or near the moment of death, expressing a final summary of insight, practice, or attitude toward the act of dying. The genre's doctrinal content varies by tradition but its formal structure is consistent: the poem is a parting utterance, performed under the pressure of imminent death, and is preserved as a kind of testament that compresses the speaker's life and understanding into a single artifact. In the Zen monastic tradition the genre carries particular weight as a final demonstration of realized understanding — the master whose insight is genuine should be able to express it in the act of dying, and the death poem becomes a final dokusan in which the assembly is the witness. Celebrated examples are preserved in the recorded sayings (語録) of major Zen masters: Dōgen's death poem, Bassui's, Hakuin's, and many others are doctrinally read as final articulations of each master's distinctive teaching. The genre also extends into the samurai tradition, where the death poem becomes a conventionalized component of seppuku (ritual suicide) and the warrior's preparation for battle, and into the broader literary culture, where Bashō's death haiku — 旅に病んで夢は枯野をかけ廻る (sick on a journey, my dreams wander the withered fields) — stands as one of the most celebrated examples in Japanese literary history. The genre's persistence across centuries reflects a particular Japanese sensibility about the relationship between artistic form and the moment of death: the death poem is neither a confession nor a spiritual will but a final aesthetic act, a last formal utterance that completes the speaker's life as a structured composition rather than allowing it to dissipate inarticulately into death.

gloss: dependent origination — the doctrine that all phenomena arise through the convergence of conditioning relations rather than through any inherent self-existence; the structural logic of conditioned arising that grounds the Buddhist analysis of suffering, the Madhyamaka analysis of emptiness, and the Mahāyāna account of interdependence
notes: Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda is one of the most foundational technical terms in the entire Buddhist vocabulary, naming the doctrine that all phenomena arise through the convergence of conditioning relations rather than through any inherent self-existence. The compound is built from pratītya (depending on, in dependence upon — gerund of prati-i, to go toward, to depend on) and samutpāda (arising-together, co-arising — sam- prefix marking convergence + utpāda, arising), and the literal sense is 'arising-in-dependence' or 'co-arising-through-conditions.' The doctrinal content operates at multiple levels of generality. At the most basic level the doctrine asserts that no phenomenon arises independently — every coming-into-being is the convergence of conditioning factors, and the phenomenon that arises is itself a relational pattern rather than a self-subsisting substance. At the more specific Abhidharma level the doctrine is articulated through the twelve-link chain (十二因縁, dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) tracing the causal sequence from ignorance (avidyā) through the formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old-age-and-death — the structural analysis of how suffering arises and how its conditions can be unraveled. At the Mahāyāna and Madhyamaka level the doctrine becomes the basis for the analysis of emptiness (śūnyatā, 空): if all phenomena arise through conditioning relations, then no phenomenon has svabhāva (inherent self-existence), and the conclusion is that all phenomena are empty — emptiness being not a substance but the relational structure of all conditioned arising. Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā develops this identification systematically, with the celebrated formula identifying pratītyasamutpāda with śūnyatā with the Middle Way. The Chinese 縁起 (Ch. yuánqǐ, Jp. engi) is a calque that pairs 縁 (conditioning ties) with 起 (arising) to preserve the relational-arising structure of the Sanskrit. The compound is doctrinally precise but generates additional registers in East Asian Buddhist usage. The Huayan tradition develops 縁起 into the elaborate doctrine of dharmadhātu-pratītyasamutpāda (法界縁起), the doctrine that the entire dharma-realm is a single web of mutual conditioning in which each phenomenon contains and reflects all others — the Indra's net image. The Zen tradition inherits the doctrine but tends to deploy it less elaborately than the scholastic schools, with the doctrinal weight of conditioned arising operating through compounds like 因縁 (innen, cause-and-condition) rather than through extended exegesis of the twelve links. The compound 縁起 also acquires a popular register in Japanese as 'omen' or 'auspicious sign' — a folk extension that retains the sense of conditioning relations but loses the technical doctrinal precision; the popular register is widespread but doctrinally derivative.

gloss: non-dual, not-two — the Mahāyāna doctrinal claim that ordinary mind's binary divisions (subject-object, saṃsāra-nirvāṇa, defilement-purity, self-other) are not ultimate features of reality but provisional structures whose suspension is constitutive of awakened insight; not the assertion of monistic unity but the suspension of the dualistic frame altogether
notes: Sanskrit advaya (a- privative + dvaya, the two — 'not two, not double, non-dual') and the closely related advaita (a- + dvaita, duality — 'non-dual') are the Mahāyāna technical terms for the suspension of the binary structure by which ordinary mind grasps phenomena. The doctrinal content is precise and easily misunderstood. Non-duality is not the assertion of monistic unity (which would itself be a dualistic move, opposing one to two) but the suspension of the binary frame altogether — the refusal to let the structure of subject-and-object, saṃsāra-and-nirvāṇa, defilement-and-purity, self-and-other settle as ultimate features of reality. The Sanskrit grammar makes the negative-theological logic explicit: advaya is built as the negation (a-) of duality (dvaya) without supplying a positive substitute, and the term names what the Mahāyāna analysis sees through rather than what it puts in place of the binary structure. The Chinese 不二 (Ch. bù'èr, Jp. funi) is a calque preserving the negation-of-duality structure: 不 (not) plus 二 (two) yields the same negative-theological compound as the Sanskrit. The doctrine receives its most concentrated articulation in the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra's celebrated 'Dharma-gate of Non-duality' (不二法門, advaya-dharma-mukha) chapter, in which a series of bodhisattvas articulate non-duality through successive negations of dualistic distinctions (production-and-cessation, defilement-and-purity, self-and-not-self, and so on). Mañjuśrī then offers a higher-order articulation: non-duality is the absence of all such formulations, the refusal to articulate at all. Vimalakīrti is asked to give the highest articulation and responds with silence — the celebrated 'thunderous silence of Vimalakīrti' that becomes one of the most famous teaching moments in Mahāyāna literature. The doctrinal stake is that non-duality cannot be articulated positively without falling back into the dualistic frame it suspends; the only adequate expression is the suspension of expression itself. The doctrine is foundational across all Mahāyāna schools and operates across many compounds: 二諦 (nitai, the two truths — conventional and ultimate) names the standard scholastic articulation in which the two truths are themselves not-two; 不二一如 (funi ichinyo) compounds non-duality with suchness; 色即是空 (form is precisely emptiness) is a non-dual identification expressed in copula form. The Chan/Zen tradition inherits and radicalizes the doctrine, with Huineng's Platform Sutra teaching the non-duality of meditation and wisdom (定慧不二) as the structural principle of the Southern school, and koans throughout the tradition operating as devices for breaking the dualistic frame. The compound 不二 carries the doctrinal weight of this entire tradition in compact form.

gloss: oneness-suchness — the fundamental non-dual identity of all phenomena in their true nature; the positive-affirmative complement to 不二's negative-theological logic, asserting unity-in-suchness rather than refusing duality
notes: 一如 (Ch. yīrú, Jp. ichinyo) is a Sino-Japanese doctrinal compound formed from 一 (one, single, identical) and 如 (thusness, just-as — the rendering of Sanskrit tathā). The compound has no single Sanskrit antecedent; it is a Chinese-Buddhist coinage that articulates the positive-affirmative side of the non-dual logic that 不二 (advaya) names negatively. Where 不二 negates the binary frame of ordinary cognition without supplying a positive substitute, 一如 affirms the single-suchness that holds across apparent multiplicity — the doctrinal claim that all phenomena are not-two by being one in their thusness. The Sanskrit referent that comes closest is ekarasa ('one-flavored, of single taste'), the Mahāyāna metaphor for the uniform suchness of all dharmas in awakened seeing, but the Chinese compound is a stand-alone coinage rather than a strict calque. The two compounds 不二 and 一如 are doctrinally complementary: the negative and positive articulations of the same non-dual logic. They are sometimes paired into the four-character compound 不二一如 (funi ichinyo, non-dual oneness-suchness) to hold both registers together. The compound carries doctrinal weight across the Mahāyāna tradition. In Tendai it underwrites the doctrine of the three-thousand-worlds-in-a-moment-of-thought (一念三千) and the three truths (三諦) that are not three but one. In Huayan it underwrites the dharma-realm of mutual interpenetration. In Chan/Zen it operates in compact compounds like 身心一如 (shinjin ichinyo, body-mind as one), Dōgen's articulation of the non-dual identity of physical and mental experience that is foundational to Sōtō embodied practice; in 自他一如 (jita ichinyo, self-and-other as one); in 迷悟一如 (meigo ichinyo, delusion-and-awakening as one); and in many other doctrinal pairings where the non-dual identity of two apparently distinct registers is at stake. The compound has no precise English equivalent; standard renderings include 'oneness,' 'suchness-as-one,' 'the one suchness,' and 'oneness-thusness,' each emphasizing a different aspect of the dual structure of the term. The doctrinal precision of the compound is essential to the entire Mahāyāna non-dual architecture and easily lost in popular presentations that collapse 一如 into generic monism.

term: rūpaṃ śūnyatā / sè jí shì kōng
gloss: form is precisely emptiness — the Heart Sutra's cardinal identity formula, expressing the non-dual identification of phenomenal appearance with emptiness; the doctrinal heart of the Prajñāpāramitā corpus
notes: The Sanskrit formula 'rūpaṃ śūnyatā śūnyataiva rūpam' ('form is emptiness; emptiness is itself form') is one of the most celebrated articulations in the entire Mahāyāna doctrinal corpus, occurring in the Heart Sutra (Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya) as the doctrinal compression of the Prajñāpāramitā teaching that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence. The Chinese rendering 色即是空、空即是色 (sè jí shì kōng, kōng jí shì sè; Jp. shiki soku ze kū, kū soku ze shiki) preserves the chiastic identity-structure through the copula 即是 ('is precisely identical with'), which functions in the formula as the assertion of non-mediated identity rather than mediated relation. The doctrinal stake is the Madhyamaka-Prajñāpāramitā position on the relationship between phenomenal appearance and emptiness: form (rūpa, the first of the five aggregates, naming the entire domain of physical-sensible phenomena) is not separate from emptiness (śūnyatā, the absence of inherent self-existence in all phenomena) and emptiness is not separate from form. The two are not two related things but one identical reality articulated under two registers. The chiastic structure is doctrinally precise: the first half ('form is emptiness') corrects the naive realist attachment to phenomenal appearance as ultimate; the second half ('emptiness is form') corrects the nihilistic misreading of emptiness as a void apart from phenomena. Together the chiasmus suspends both extremes — the eternalist reification of phenomena and the nihilist denial of phenomena — by asserting their non-dual identity. The formula is the most concentrated articulation of the Mahāyāna middle way (中道, madhyama-pratipad) in compact form. The Heart Sutra continues with parallel formulations for the remaining four aggregates ('feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise empty'), extending the doctrinal claim across the entire psychophysical complex. The formula is the doctrinal heart of the Prajñāpāramitā corpus and one of the most recited and commented-upon passages in all of East Asian Buddhism.

gloss: dharma-realm, the totality of phenomena understood as a single interpenetrating whole; the all-encompassing reality of the awakened dharma-vision; the foundational concept of Huayan totality-philosophy
notes: Sanskrit dharmadhātu is a compound of dharma (the elements of phenomenal reality, in the Abhidharma analysis; later, the totality of phenomena and their nature) and dhātu (element, realm, sphere, ultimate constituent). The compound has two registers in Buddhist usage. In the earlier Abhidharma stratum dharmadhātu names one of the eighteen elements (十八界) — the dharma-element that is the object of mind-consciousness, paralleling the visible-element that is the object of eye-consciousness, the audible-element that is the object of ear-consciousness, and so on. In the later Mahāyāna stratum, especially as articulated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra (華厳経) and systematized by the Huayan masters Dushun, Zhiyan, Fazang, Chengguan, and Zongmi, dharmadhātu becomes the all-encompassing realm of all phenomena understood as a single interpenetrating whole — the awakened-vision totality of which each phenomenon is a fully expressive instance. The Chinese rendering 法界 (Ch. fǎjiè, Jp. hokkai) preserves this double structure: 法 (dharma, phenomena) plus 界 (dhātu, realm/element) yields a compound that operates in both Abhidharma-analytical and Mahāyāna-cosmological senses. The Huayan tradition articulates the dharmadhātu through the celebrated Fourfold Dharmadhātu doctrine: 事法界 (the realm of phenomena), 理法界 (the realm of principle), 理事無礙法界 (the realm of unobstructed interpenetration of principle and phenomenon), 事事無礙法界 (the realm of unobstructed interpenetration of phenomenon and phenomenon). The fourth and highest articulation — 事事無礙 — is the Huayan signature claim: each particular phenomenon contains and reflects all other phenomena without obstruction, the totality fully expressed in each part. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra's celebrated metaphor of Indra's Net (帝網, Indra-jāla) — a cosmic net of jewels in which each jewel reflects every other jewel and the reflection of every other jewel in every other jewel, in infinite recursion — stages this doctrine in concrete imagery. The dharmadhātu doctrine is one of the foundational frames of East Asian Mahāyāna doctrine and pervades Chan/Zen discourse, often as a tacit cosmological background to claims about non-duality, mutual interpenetration, and the totality of reality being expressed in each particular moment.

gloss: unobstructed interpenetration of phenomenon with phenomenon — the highest of the Huayan fourfold dharmadhātu, asserting that each particular thing contains and reflects all others without mutual obstruction
notes: 事事無礙 (Ch. shìshì wú'ài, Jp. jijimuge) is a Huayan technical compound that is the highest of the Fourfold Dharmadhātu (四法界) doctrine systematized by Fazang and Chengguan. The compound is built from doubled 事 (phenomenon, particular event) plus 無 (no, without) plus 礙 (obstruction): 'phenomenon and phenomenon, without obstruction.' The doctrinal claim is precise. The Fourfold Dharmadhātu articulates four registers of the awakened dharma-vision: the realm of phenomena (事法界), the realm of principle (理法界), the realm of unobstructed interpenetration of principle and phenomenon (理事無礙法界), and the realm of unobstructed interpenetration of phenomenon and phenomenon (事事無礙法界). The first three registers structure the relationship between phenomena and the principle that pervades them; the fourth register makes the radical claim that each phenomenon, just in its concrete particularity, contains and reflects every other phenomenon without obstruction — the totality is fully expressed in each part, and each part is fully expressive of every other part. The doctrine has no exact Sanskrit antecedent; it is a Sino-Buddhist scholastic articulation developed by the Huayan masters from the imagery and conceptual resources of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra (華厳経, Buddhāvataṃsaka), particularly the Sūtra's celebrated metaphor of Indra's Net (帝網, Indra-jāla) — the cosmic net of jewels in which each jewel reflects every other jewel and the reflection of every other jewel in every other jewel, in infinite recursion without mutual obstruction. The doctrine is foundational to Huayan totality-philosophy and pervades East Asian Mahāyāna discourse beyond the Huayan school proper. The Tiantai/Tendai tradition develops a closely related doctrine of the three-thousand-worlds-in-a-moment-of-thought (一念三千). The Chan/Zen tradition inherits the doctrine as a tacit cosmological background and explicit reference point for claims about the interpenetration of all phenomena, the totality of reality being expressed in each particular moment of practice, and the non-obstruction of all things in awakened seeing. Dōgen invokes the doctrine across the Shōbōgenzō, particularly in fascicles concerning being-time (有時) and the manifest fundamental point (現成公案), where the simultaneous totality of all things in each moment is the doctrinal stake. The doctrine carries the entire weight of the Huayan totality-vision in compact form, and English renderings (interpenetration, mutual non-obstruction, the unobstructed interpenetration of phenomenon with phenomenon) all attempt to convey the dual structure of the compound: each phenomenon fully itself, and each phenomenon fully expressive of all others, without contradiction.

gloss: the unborn — the dharma-nature articulated by negation of the verbal noun of arising; the absolute reality in which there is no coming-into-being and therefore no passing-away
notes: anutpāda (Sanskrit, the privative an- attached to the verbal noun utpāda 'arising'; Chinese 不生 bùshēng, Japanese fushō) is a Mahāyāna technical concept articulating the dharma-nature from the side of negation. The compound is built from the privative prefix and a verbal noun, and the resulting form does not name a positive state of unbornness but the active suspension of the conceptual frame of arising-and-perishing. In Madhyamaka philosophy the unborn is articulated through Nāgārjuna's celebrated negation of the four extremes of arising — phenomena do not arise from themselves, from another, from both, nor without cause — and this negative-theological articulation is foundational across the Prajñāpāramitā literature. The Heart Sutra's celebrated cascade 不生不滅、不垢不浄、不増不減 (not arising, not ceasing; not defiled, not pure; not increasing, not decreasing) deploys 不生 as the first member of the cascade through which the nature of dharmas is articulated by sustained negation. The Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra develops the unborn in connection with Buddha-nature and the tathāgatagarbha cluster of texts. The doctrine acquires a distinctive practical-existential register in the teaching of Bankei Yōtaku (1622–1693), the Edo-period Rinzai master whose entire teaching career centers on the unborn (不生 fushō): Bankei taught that the buddha-mind is the unborn, that the unborn is fully present and fully functioning in each ordinary moment of awareness, and that practice consists not in koan introspection or scholastic study but in abiding in the unborn rather than slipping into the produced and conditioned states of self-concern, anger, and discriminative thought. Bankei's unborn is doctrinally continuous with the Madhyamaka articulation but registrally distinctive: where Madhyamaka articulates the unborn through scholastic negation, Bankei points to the unborn directly as the present functioning of awareness, an ordinary-language pedagogy aimed at lay students and farmers as well as monastics.

gloss: principle — the absolute, universal, undifferentiated dimension of reality; the patterning that pervades all phenomena, paired against 事 (phenomena, the concrete particular) in the Huayan dialectic
notes: 理 (Chinese lǐ, Japanese ri) is a native Chinese philosophical concept whose technical use as the principle-pole of the 理事 dialectic is articulated by the Huayan masters of the Tang dynasty (Dushun, Fazang, Chengguan) and inherited across the Chinese and Japanese Buddhist traditions. The character's pre-Buddhist semantic core is the natural pattern of veins running through jade — the patterning that the jade-worker reads off the stone and cuts along — and this concrete sense extends in classical Chinese philosophical usage to the ordering principle that pervades all things. In the Huayan articulation of the Fourfold Dharmadhātu doctrine 理 names the absolute, universal, undifferentiated dimension of reality, paired against 事 (the concrete, particular, differentiated dimension); the four registers of the dharmadhātu — the realm of phenomena, the realm of principle, the realm of unobstructed interpenetration of principle and phenomenon, the realm of unobstructed interpenetration of phenomenon and phenomenon — articulate progressively higher configurations of the relationship between these two poles. The Caodong/Sōtō tradition's Five Ranks (五位) of Dongshan Liangjie inherit the 理事 dialectic and articulate the relationships between absolute (正 shō) and relative (偏 hen) through five distinct configurations of the principle-and-phenomenon relation, with the Five Ranks structure operating as the underlying conceptual scaffold for much subsequent koan commentary in both Caodong/Sōtō and Linji/Rinzai. Shitou Xiqian's Sandōkai (参同契) is the foundational verse-doctrinal articulation of the 理事 dialectic in the Caodong tradition, transmitted through Shitou's lineage to Dongshan and inherited by Dōgen's Sōtō transmission to Japan. The Neo-Confucian reception of 理 — particularly in the Cheng-Zhu school — articulates 理 as the cosmological-ethical ordering principle of the natural and moral order, and the Buddhist and Neo-Confucian uses of the term remain doctrinally distinct but historically interpenetrating across East Asian intellectual discourse.

gloss: phenomena, particulars, concrete events — the differentiated dimension of reality, paired against 理 (principle) in the Huayan dialectic; each phenomenon fully itself in its concrete particularity
notes: 事 (Chinese shì, Japanese ji) is the technical Huayan and Chan/Zen term for the concrete-particular dimension of reality, paired against 理 (principle, the absolute-universal). The character's pre-Buddhist semantic core is the act of taking up an office or undertaking a duty (the oracle-bone form depicts a hand grasping a banner of office), and from this concrete sense the character extends in classical Chinese to: matter, business, affair, occupation, occurrence — anything that is taken in hand or undertaken. The Huayan technical use of 事 deploys this semantic register of concrete-particular occurrence as the doctrinal name for the differentiated phenomena that compose the dharma-realm. In the Fourfold Dharmadhātu doctrine the four progressively higher articulations of the dharmadhātu — the realm of phenomena (事法界), the realm of principle (理法界), the realm of unobstructed interpenetration of principle and phenomenon (理事無礙法界), and the realm of unobstructed interpenetration of phenomenon and phenomenon (事事無礙法界) — culminate in the radical claim that each phenomenon, just in its concrete particularity, contains and reflects all other phenomena without obstruction. The doctrinal stake of 事 in this culminating register is precise: each particular thing remains fully itself, distinct in its concrete particularity, and yet expresses the totality without remainder; the Huayan analysis works out the structure of this dual condition with extraordinary scholastic care. The Caodong/Sōtō Five Ranks tradition inherits the 理事 dialectic and articulates the relationships between absolute (正 shō) and relative (偏 hen) through five distinct configurations, with 事 operating as the side of the relative-particular in the Five-Ranks scheme. Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō appropriates the 理事 vocabulary across multiple fascicles, with the Genjōkōan fascicle's title (現成公案) deploying the doctrinal weight of 事 in compact form: the koan is not a principle to be grasped but the present concrete event in which practice-realization is enacted.

gloss: casting off body-mind — the falling-away of the body-and-mind structure as the moment of awakening; Dōgen's name for the pivotal awakening event that occurred under his Chinese master Tiantong Rujing
notes: 身心脱落 is doctrinally a Dōgen-Sōtō technical term mediated through Dōgen's Chinese master Tiantong Rujing (天童如浄, 1163–1228) at Mt. Tendō (天童山) in 1227. The traditional account, preserved across Dōgen's writings and the Sōtō hagiographical tradition, narrates the moment as follows: during morning zazen Rujing rebukes a sleeping monk with the phrase 参禅は須らく身心脱落なるべし — 'the study of Zen requires nothing other than the casting off of body-mind' — and Dōgen, hearing the phrase, attains the awakening that makes him the Sōtō patriarch in Japan. The phrase's authenticity as Rujing's actual words has been contested by modern scholarship — there is some textual evidence that Dōgen's transcription of Rujing's saying may involve the related compound 心塵脱落 (shinjin datsuraku, casting off the dust of the heart-mind) rather than 身心脱落, and the homophony of the two compounds in Japanese pronunciation has been exploited by Dōgen as a doctrinal hinge. Whatever the historical-textual situation, the Dōgen-Sōtō tradition has uniformly received the term as 身心脱落 (the casting off of body-and-mind, with 身 as the body), and the doctrinal articulation across the Shōbōgenzō (particularly in the Genjōkōan, Bendōwa, and Busshō fascicles) deploys the compound in its body-mind reading. The compound's doctrinal precision is in the calibrated grammar of release-without-destruction: the body-mind structure falls away, but the body-mind themselves remain, in unobstructed functioning. Dōgen's awakening-grammar is calibrated against any acquisition-grammar in which awakening is the gaining of a new condition: 脱落 names a falling-off, a structural release, that leaves the body-mind in their full and proper functioning rather than annihilating them.

gloss: being-time — the radical identity of existence and time; all beings are time, all time is being; Dōgen's title for one of the most philosophically dense fascicles of the Shōbōgenzō
notes: 有時 is one of the most philosophically dense compounds in Dōgen's vocabulary, articulated in the Shōbōgenzō Uji fascicle composed in 1240. The compound exploits the polysemy of 有 (existence, being, having) and 時 (time, the moment, the occasion) to articulate the doctrinal claim that being and time are inseparable — that every being is the timing of its being, and every time is the being of its timing. Dōgen's articulation in the Uji fascicle works out the implications across multiple registers: the mountain is time, the standing-on-the-summit is time, the monk passing through the marketplace is time. Each particular being is the temporal articulation through which it occurs, and time is not the receptacle in which beings appear but the very mode of their articulation. The compound is structurally distinct from any container-conception of time (time as the receptacle of beings) and from any extrusion-conception of time (time as what flows past the static observer). The doctrinal antecedents are in the Mahāyāna scriptural articulation of impermanence, in the Tiantai/Tendai treatment of the moment-of-thought (一念 ichinen), and in the Huayan doctrine of the mutual interpenetration of the ten times (十世) — but Dōgen's articulation is technically distinct from all of these and constitutes one of the most original philosophical contributions of the East Asian Buddhist tradition. The compound has become — particularly through the modern reception of Dōgen's philosophy in twentieth-century Japanese and Western philosophy (Tanabe Hajime, Watsuji Tetsurō, Heidegger-influenced readings, and the work of Hee-Jin Kim and others) — one of the central reference points for cross-cultural philosophical dialogue about the nature of time.

gloss: the manifest fundamental point — reality as the present already-accomplished koan; Dōgen's title for the first and most celebrated fascicle of the Shōbōgenzō
notes: 現成公案 is one of the most precisely calibrated compounds in Dōgen's technical vocabulary. The compound 現成 (genjō) deploys 現 (manifestation, becoming present) and 成 (completion, becoming) together to name the present-already-accomplished condition: the manifestation that is simultaneously already complete in its standing-forth. The compound 公案 (kōan) carries the Tang-dynasty legal sense of the magistrate's official case-file as inherited by the Chan/Zen tradition for the recorded encounters of the ancestors. Together the four characters articulate Dōgen's doctrinal claim: reality as it stands forth at this moment is itself the koan, the case to be encountered, the precedent to be received. The koan is not a problem to be solved nor a hidden truth to be uncovered but the present moment of practice-realization itself, fully manifest and already complete in its standing-forth. The fascicle of the same title — composed in 1233 as a letter to a lay disciple, Yō Kōshū, and revised across Dōgen's career — is the first fascicle of the 75-fascicle Shōbōgenzō and one of the most widely commented texts in the Sōtō tradition. The fascicle's celebrated opening lines articulate the dialectic of practice-realization across multiple registers (when all things are dharma, there is delusion and awakening; when all things are without self, there is neither delusion nor awakening) and develop the doctrinal claim that reality stands forth as the koan in the structure of practice-realization itself. The fascicle is taken across the Sōtō tradition as the most concentrated articulation of Dōgen's philosophical position and is treated as the doctrinal key to the rest of the Shōbōgenzō.

gloss: non-thinking — the awareness that includes and exceeds both thinking and not-thinking; the proper mode of mental activity in zazen, articulated by Dōgen in the Fukanzazengi after Yaoshan's Tang-dynasty dialogue
notes: 非思量 is doctrinally the Sōtō technical term for the proper mode of awareness in zazen, articulated centrally in Dōgen's Fukanzazengi (普勧坐禅儀, Universal Recommendation of Zazen) and the Zazenshin fascicle of the Shōbōgenzō. The term is not Dōgen's coinage but his appropriation of a Tang-dynasty dialogue between Yaoshan Weiyan (薬山惟儼, 745–828) and an unnamed monk, preserved in the Jingde Chuandeng Lu and other Chan recorded-sayings collections. The dialogue runs: a monk asks Yaoshan, sitting in steadfast composure, what he is thinking; Yaoshan answers that he thinks the non-thinkable (思量箇不思量底); the monk asks how one thinks the non-thinkable; Yaoshan answers 非思量 (non-thinking). The exchange distinguishes three registers: 思量 (shiryō, thinking) names the active discursive register; 不思量 (fushiryō, not-thinking) names the privative absence of thinking; 非思量 (hishiryō, non-thinking) names a third register that is neither thinking nor its mere absence but the awareness in which thinking arises and falls away without being either deployed or suppressed. The doctrinal precision is in 非's function as the negation of identity rather than the negation of presence: hishiryō is not the absence of thinking but the absence of the X-is-thinking structure, the suspension of the predicative grammar that constitutes ordinary mental activity. Dōgen's appropriation of the Yaoshan dialogue in the Fukanzazengi makes hishiryō the doctrinal anchor of the Sōtō articulation of zazen-awareness, and the term has remained the central reference point for the Sōtō tradition's distinctive handling of the question of mental activity in seated meditation.

gloss: the oneness of practice and realization — Dōgen's principle that practice does not lead to a separate enlightenment but is itself the active expression of realization; the structural identity of cultivation and awakened verification
notes: 修証一等 is one of the central doctrinal articulations of Dōgen's Sōtō transmission, named in the Bendōwa (弁道話, On the Endeavor of the Way; 1231) and elaborated across the Shōbōgenzō. The compound articulates the doctrinal claim that 修 (cultivation, practice) and 証 (realization, verification) are not two distinct stages of the path — first practice as means, then realization as result — but a single structural condition with two distinguishable poles. Dōgen's calibration of the relationship is precise: practice is not the means by which realization is later produced; realization is not the inert content that practice merely awaits. Rather, practice is the present-active mode in which realization is realized, and realization is the awakened condition that practice is the temporal-active expression of. The doctrinal stake of the compound is structural: it dismantles the means-end grammar that would make zazen a technique for producing satori at some later moment, and replaces it with the practice-realization unity in which every moment of zazen is itself the awakened activity of the buddhas and ancestors. Dōgen articulates the doctrine in the Bendōwa against a position he characterizes as a fundamental misunderstanding of both practice and realization — the position that practice is unnecessary for those who have already attained realization. The compound has remained the central doctrinal formula of Sōtō practice-theory across the eight centuries since Dōgen's articulation and is the doctrinal anchor for the Sōtō understanding of zazen as not a means to enlightenment but the active presence of enlightenment itself. The compound's structural relations to other Dōgen-coined terms are integral: 修証一等 is structurally continuous with 現成公案 (the manifest fundamental point) in identifying the present moment as the locus of realization; with 自受用三昧 (jijuyū zanmai, self-receiving samādhi) in identifying zazen as a self-fulfilling activity; and with 行持 (gyōji, continuous practice) in identifying the temporal extension of practice-realization as unbroken activity rather than episodic technique.

gloss: able to express the Way — Dōgen's name for authentic articulation of awakened understanding through words, actions, and silence; the modal-postverbal construction V+得 marking the capacity to say the Way rather than the acquisition of the Way as object
notes: 道得 is one of the most distinctive of Dōgen's technical terms, articulated centrally in the Dōtoku (道得) fascicle of the Shōbōgenzō (composed 1242). The compound exploits the classical Chinese modal-postverbal construction V+得 — in which 得 marks the capacity or successful completion of the verbal action — to make 道 (here functioning verbally, 'to say, to articulate, to speak') the verb whose successful articulation 得 marks. The compound is therefore not 'to attain the Way' (which would treat 道 as a substantival object of acquisition) but 'to be able to say the Way, to manage to articulate the Way, to successfully express the Way.' The doctrinal stake of the construction is precise: Dōgen is naming the capacity for authentic articulation of the awakened understanding, the linguistic-expressive dimension of the practice-realization unity that the wider Shōbōgenzō articulates. The Dōtoku fascicle treats 道得 across several registers: the buddhas and ancestors are characterized by their capacity to 道得 (articulate the Way), and this capacity is not a separate ornament added to their realization but the active-linguistic dimension of the realization itself. The doctrinal argument of the fascicle is in part a polemic against a position that would relegate words to a secondary register (as expedient pointers to a supposedly wordless awakening): Dōgen insists, against this view, that 道得 is the active mode in which the buddhas and ancestors are buddhas and ancestors. The compound has structural relations to a complementary Dōgen articulation, 不道得 (not-able-to-say) and 道不得 (saying-not-able), which the fascicle articulates as the dialectical complements of 道得 — the buddhas and ancestors are equally characterized by what they can articulate and by what their articulation cannot exhaust. The compound has been central to modern Sōtō scholarship's interest in Dōgen's philosophy of language, with major treatments by Hee-Jin Kim, Steven Heine, Tom Kasulis, and others articulating Dōgen's position as a sophisticated philosophy of religious language that resists the standard Buddhist suspicion of words while preserving a register of doctrinal precision the Western philosophy of language has rarely matched.

gloss: the Five Ranks — Dongshan Liangjie's framework articulating the dialectical relationship between the absolute (正, shō) and the relative (偏, hen) across five distinct structural positions; foundational to both Sōtō and Rinzai koan curricula
notes: 五位 (Wǔwèi, goi) is the systematic doctrinal framework articulated by Dongshan Liangjie (洞山良价, 807–869), founder of the Caodong (J. Sōtō) lineage of Chinese Chan, naming the dialectical relationship between the absolute (正, shō; Ch. zhèng) and the relative (偏, hen; Ch. piān) across five distinct structural positions. The five ranks are: 正中偏 (the relative within the absolute) — the absolute is the structural ground from which the relative differentiations arise; 偏中正 (the absolute within the relative) — the absolute is encountered within and through the relative differentiations; 正中来 (coming-from-within-the-absolute) — the bodhisattva-activity that issues from the absolute into the world of phenomena; 偏中至 (arrival-within-the-relative, sometimes 兼中至, mutual-arrival) — the integrative position in which the absolute-relative articulation is fully expressed; 兼中到 (attainment-of-mutual-integration) — the consummative position in which the dialectical movement is brought to completion.
