The decisive coinage moment was the 1873 Vienna World Exposition (Wiener Weltausstellung), where the Meiji government required a Japanese rendering of the German exhibition category bildende Kunst to organize the Japanese pavilion's submissions, and the term 美術 was adopted in the official translation of the German exhibition regulations (Kunstwerke, Kunstgewerbe, etc.) — the institutional moment at which the Western category of 'fine art' was first imposed on Japanese practice and a Japanese word coined to name it. Re-exported to Chinese (měishù) and Korean (misul) as the standard term.

gloss: literature as the modern Western category of imaginative written art — poetry, drama, the novel, the essay — conceived as a bounded aesthetic-cultural domain with its own canon, history, and critical-academic discipline (literary criticism, literary history, comparative literature); distinct from the older inclusive sense of 'letters' (belles-lettres, gelehrte Literatur) covering all polite written learning, and from the philological-text-critical scholarship of the classical philological tradition
notes: The modern Western disciplinary concept of literature was constituted across the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries through the Romantic valorization of the imaginative work, the consolidation of the national literary canon (German Nationalliteratur, English literature, French littérature nationale), and the academic institutionalization of the literary disciplines in the late-nineteenth-century European university. The classical Chinese compound 文学 (wénxué) had long meant 'the cultivation of letters / literary learning' in the broad Confucian sense (one of the four subjects under Confucius, 孔門四科), but had not named an aesthetic-imaginative domain. Meiji translators recoined 文学 in its modern sense through the establishment of the bungakubu (faculty of letters) at Tokyo Imperial University in 1877 and through critical works of the 1880s — most decisively Tsubouchi Shōyō's Shōsetsu Shinzui (1885–86), which argued for the novel (小説, shōsetsu) as a serious aesthetic genre and inaugurated modern Japanese literary criticism. Re-exported to Chinese (wénxué) and Korean (munhak) as the standard modern term for literature as a discipline.

gloss: art as the modern Western aesthetic-philosophical category — the unified domain of skilled aesthetic production across the various media (visual, plastic, literary, musical, performative), conceived as autonomous from mere craft, utility, and entertainment, and constituted by the eighteenth-century systematization of the arts and the nineteenth-century aesthetics of the autonomous artwork; in Kant and the post-Kantian tradition (Critique of the Power of Judgment, Schiller, Schelling, Hegel's Aesthetics) the central category of philosophical aesthetics
notes: A Western category constituted by Renaissance through eighteenth-century reflection (Vasari, Batteux, Kant) and given philosophical-aesthetic depth in the post-Kantian tradition. The category names something more general than 'the fine arts' (美術): art as the totality of cultivated aesthetic production across all media, understood as a coherent conceptual sphere. Pre-Meiji Japan had no equivalent unifying term; the various arts were classified under their specific media (絵画 painting, 彫刻 sculpture, 音楽 music, 詩 poetry, 演劇 drama) without a single concept binding them as 'art.' The Meiji coinage 芸術 — combining 芸 (cultivated capacity, the traditional 六藝 'six arts') with 術 (trained procedure) — was stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and Mori Ōgai's aesthetic writings of the 1890s as the term for art in this unified Kantian-aesthetic sense, distinct from the narrower 美術 (fine arts as institutional domain). The pair 芸術 / 美術 lets modern Japanese carry roughly the German Kunst / bildende Kunst distinction. Re-exported to Chinese (yìshù 艺术) and Korean (yesul 예술).

gloss: history as the modern Western academic discipline of the critical-evidentiary reconstruction of the human past — Rankean source-criticism, periodization, the construction of national and world histories, the institutional apparatus of the university history department, the archive, and the scholarly historical monograph; distinct from the older indigenous East Asian tradition of dynastic chronicle and the Confucian moral-evaluative historiography of the standard histories (正史)
notes: The modern Western academic discipline of history was constituted across the nineteenth century by Leopold von Ranke's source-critical method (Geschichten der romanischen und germanischen Völker, 1824, with its famous 'wie es eigentlich gewesen'), by the development of the seminar method at German universities (Berlin, Göttingen), by the rise of national-historical projects, and by the institutionalization of history as a university discipline distinct from chronicle, antiquarianism, and the philosophy of history. East Asia possessed an enormous indigenous historiographical tradition — Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (史記), the twenty-four standard dynastic histories, the Mirror Comprehensive in Aid of Governance (資治通鑑), the Japanese rikkokushi (六国史) — but this tradition was organized around the chronicle (編年体) and the standard-history (紀伝体) genres and conceived under the heading 史 (the scribe's record) rather than 歴史 as an academic discipline. The Meiji compound 歴史 was stabilized as the modern academic term through the establishment of the Tokyo Imperial University history department in 1887 (under Ludwig Riess, brought from Germany to introduce Rankean method), through Naka Michiyo's foundational works (Shina Tsūshi 支那通史, 1888–1890; the periodization of East Asian history into ancient/medieval/modern), and through the broader Meiji project of writing Japan and East Asia into world-historical narratives. Re-exported to Chinese (lìshǐ) and Korean (yeoksa 역사) as the standard modern term.

gloss: psychology as the modern Western academic discipline of mind — the systematic, methodologically-self-conscious study of mental phenomena (sensation, perception, cognition, emotion, will, the unconscious) conceived as a bounded scientific-academic field, distinct on one side from the older speculative philosophy of mind (faculty psychology in the rationalist tradition, the Lockean theory of ideas, the Kantian transcendental psychology) and on the other from neurology and physiology; in its late-nineteenth-century formation principally the Wundtian experimental psychology of the Leipzig laboratory (1879) and the broader continental psychological tradition that emerged from it
notes: The modern Western discipline of psychology was constituted in the second half of the nineteenth century through the convergence of three previously distinct traditions: the older speculative philosophy of mind (the faculty psychology of the Scottish common-sense school, the Lockean and Humean theories of ideas, the Kantian transcendental psychology), the new experimental physiology of the sense organs and the nervous system (Helmholtz, E.H. Weber, Fechner's psychophysics), and the British associationist tradition (Mill, Bain). Wilhelm Wundt's establishment of the first psychological laboratory at Leipzig in 1879 is conventionally taken as the institutional founding moment of psychology as an autonomous experimental science distinct from philosophy. The Meiji rendering 心理学 has a complex layered history. Nishi Amane introduced the compound through his foundational 1875 translation of Joseph Haven's Mental Philosophy (1857) — published under the title 心理学 — as the rendering of the American Scottish-common-sense-tradition 'mental philosophy' before the term acquired its narrower experimental-scientific sense. Motora Yūjirō, who studied under G. Stanley Hall at Johns Hopkins, returned to Japan and established Japan's first psychological laboratory at Tokyo Imperial University in 1888, importing the Wundtian experimental-scientific register and binding 心理学 to its modern academic-laboratory form. The Tetsugaku Jii (1881) stabilized 心理学 as the standing lexical equivalent of 'psychology' in its modern academic sense. Re-exported to Chinese (xīnlǐxué) and Korean (simnihak 심리학) as the standard modern term.

gloss: tragedy as the bounded Western dramatic genre — the staged drama of serious action ending in catastrophic loss, ruin, or death, with its conventional protagonist of high estate brought to fall through error, fate, or character, and its conventional cathartic effect on the audience; constituted as a genre by Greek Athenian fifth-century drama (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides) and theorized by Aristotle's Poetics; revived and transformed across Renaissance, neoclassical, Romantic, and modern European drama (Shakespeare, Racine, Schiller, Ibsen)
notes: Tragedy as a bounded dramatic genre is a specifically Western category, constituted by the Athenian dramatic festivals of the fifth century BCE (the City Dionysia, the Lenaia), theorized by Aristotle's Poetics as the imitation of serious action whose conventional plot-shape involves a fall from prosperity to misery through hamartia (error), and revived across European dramatic tradition through Senecan neoclassical tragedy, Shakespearean tragedy, French neoclassical tragedy (Corneille, Racine), German Sturm-und-Drang and Weimar classicism (Lessing, Schiller, Goethe), the Romantic and post-Romantic tragic tradition, and Ibsenite naturalist tragedy. The classical East Asian theatrical traditions had their own genre-vocabularies — the no 能, kabuki 歌舞伎, and bunraku 文楽 of Japan; the various xiqu 戯曲 forms of China — but none of these traditions had the bounded tragic genre as a distinct category, and the rendering of the Western tragic genre into Japanese required the Meiji coinage of 悲劇. The compound, stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and the broader Meiji translation of Western aesthetic-literary vocabulary, pairs 悲 (sorrow) with 劇 (drama) to mark the dramatic genre of sorrow. The reception of Western tragedy in Meiji and post-Meiji Japan unfolded across the Shingeki (新劇, 'new drama') theatrical movement, with Tsubouchi Shōyō's translations of Shakespeare (1909–1928) being the foundational Japanese-language engagement with European tragedy. Re-exported to Chinese (bēijù 悲剧) and Korean (bigeuk 비극) as the standard modern term.

gloss: comedy as the bounded Western dramatic genre — the staged drama of light or humorous action ending in resolution, marriage, or restoration, with its conventional protagonists drawn from ordinary or middling life and its conventional cathartic effect of laughter; constituted as a genre by Greek Athenian fifth-century drama (Aristophanes, Menander) and Roman New Comedy (Plautus, Terence), and developed across medieval, Renaissance, and modern European drama (commedia dell'arte, Shakespearean comedy, Molière, Restoration comedy, modern comic theatre)
notes: Comedy as a bounded dramatic genre is the structural counterpart of tragedy in Western dramatic theory, constituted by Greek Athenian Old Comedy (Aristophanes), Greek New Comedy (Menander), and the Roman comic tradition of Plautus and Terence, and developed across the medieval cyclic plays, Renaissance commedia dell'arte and Shakespearean comedy, French neoclassical comedy (Molière), Restoration comedy, and the modern European comic theatre. Aristotle's Poetics treats comedy as the imitation of the laughable in the inferior register, distinguished from tragedy by its plot-shape of resolution rather than catastrophe and by its conventional protagonists drawn from ordinary rather than noble life. As with tragedy, the bounded comic genre is not native to classical East Asian theatrical traditions, and the rendering of the Western comic genre into Japanese required the Meiji coinage of 喜劇 — pairing 喜 (joy) with 劇 (drama) to mark the dramatic genre of joy, in structural parallel with 悲劇. The compound was stabilized through the Tetsugaku Jii (1881) and the broader Meiji translation of Western aesthetic-literary vocabulary, and the reception of Western comedy in Meiji Japan unfolded alongside the reception of tragedy through the Shingeki theatrical movement and the Tsubouchi Shōyō Shakespeare translations. The genre-pair 悲劇 / 喜劇 supplies in modern East Asian theatrical vocabulary the precise structural equivalent of the Western tragedy / comedy pair, and the symmetry of the two compounds (sorrow-drama / joy-drama) renders the structural symmetry of the Western genre-distinction in compact Sino-Japanese form. Re-exported to Chinese (xǐjù 喜剧) and Korean (huigeuk 희극) as the standard modern term.
